title: Why Have Saudi Air Defenses Failed To Intercept Houthi Missiles?
desc:
Why Have Saudi Air Defenses Failed To Intercept Houthi Missiles?

Via Middle East Eye

For years, Yemen's Houthis have demonstrated their ability to strike some of Saudi Arabia's most strategically important targets, from oil infrastructure to the kingdom's capital. But repeated missile and drone strikes on Riyadh's main international airport have raised fresh questions about the limits of the kingdom's sophisticated air defenses.

Since October 6, the strikes have killed at least 20 people and injured almost 400. The deadliest attack so far happened on 10 October when 12 people were killed and more than 300 wounded.

On Monday, the kingdom vowed a "serious" response to the attacks and less than 24 hours later, Saudi strikes targeted energy facilities in Sanaa - causing massive fires and explosions that rocked the Yemeni capital.

So why have the latest Houthi attacks repeatedly penetrated Saudi defenses, and what do they reveal about the kingdom's ability to protect its most valuable assets?

Riyadh has spent billions of dollars on some of the world's most advanced air-defense systems, assembling an arsenal designed to counter precisely these threats. Its equipment includes the American-made MIM-104 Patriot, including the advanced PAC-3 variant with hit-to-kill technology, and the even more sophisticated Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) system.

Both can intercept ballistic missiles and have demonstrated their capabilities in combat. Saudi Arabia also has a well-equipped air force, including advanced F-15s and Eurofighter Typhoons, capable of engaging drones and cruise missiles.

Yet Houthi missiles and drones have repeatedly evaded or penetrated the kingdom's defenses, exposing the difficulty of protecting a vast territory and its high-value targets from sustained attacks.

Nicholas Heras, interim executive director at the Middle East Policy Council and senior director at the New Lines Institute, said Saudi Arabia's vast territory leaves it "unusually exposed" to Houthi attacks launched from northern Yemen.

"Much of Saudi territory is desert, which makes it challenging to fully defend because of the distances that must be accounted for - and it costs more to have personnel maintain early warning systems in that terrain," Heras told Middle East Eye.

"The Houthis have a target-rich environment in Saudi Arabia that includes some of the most important oil infrastructure in the world that are more immediately exposed to the drone and missile attack capabilities that the Houthis possess."

Heras said the attacks on Riyadh were intended to send a message to Saudi Arabia amid renewed fighting in Yemen.

"The Houthis perceived a gap in Saudi capability and attention span and struck Riyadh to send a signal to Saudi Arabia that if Sanaa is hit, Riyadh will be hit," he said.

'Deliberate escalation'

Federico Borsari, a defense expert at the Centre for European Policy Analysis (Cepa), believes the strikes represent an escalation in the Yemeni group’ willingness to attack the kingdom rather than necessarily demonstrating a fundamentally new capability.

The group has possessed long-range strike capabilities for almost a decade and previously targeted Riyadh in 2017. "Since then, their arsenal has further expanded to include increasingly sophisticated ballistic and cruise missiles built with Iranian help," Borsari told MEE. "But without evidence it is hard to tell whether some new capabilities were used."

For Borsari, the more concerning development "is the Houthis' ability to conduct repeated, coordinated strikes against heavily defended targets." He added that the timing appears consistent with "deliberate escalation intended to impose economic and political costs" on Saudi Arabia amid renewed fighting in Yemen.

Freddy Khoueiry, lead Middle East and North Africa and defense analyst at risk intelligence company RANE, said it remained unclear whether the attacks reflected new Houthi capabilities.

"Based on publicly available information, it is still difficult to determine whether the Riyadh attacks represent a specific new technological upgrade or simply a decision to employ existing capabilities more aggressively against civilian aviation infrastructure," he told MEE. "In either case, the escalation is significant because the Houthis are demonstrating both the capability and willingness to impose direct costs on the Saudi capital," he said.

Mohammed al-Basha of the Virginia-based Basha Report risk advisory said the Houthis had spent years refining their long-range strike capabilities. "For years, the Houthis have used their attacks on Israel to refine their long-range strike capabilities," he told MEE. "What appeared to be failed attacks were also opportunities to learn and adapt."

The group may have applied lessons from its regional attacks, as well as from Iran’s confrontations with the US and Israel, to improve its ability to challenge sophisticated air-defence networks. "Saudi Arabia has invested heavily in Patriot, Thaad, and other systems, but its vast territory makes comprehensive protection difficult," al-Basha said.

"The Houthis do not need to overwhelm the entire network. One successful strike can cause significant damage and disruption."

WATCH: Security cameras capture the terrifying moments explosions rock three airports in Saudi Arabia, sending debris crashing down inside passenger terminals. Newly released footage shows blasts near airport seating at Abha, damage to the ceiling at Jazan and debris falling inside Najran International Airport. Saudi officials blame Houthi attacks for the destruction, reporting three people killed and 28 wounded in strikes on Abha airport alone. The attacks are part of a broader campaign targeting Saudi airports, ports and oil facilities.

— Fox News (@FoxNews) October 16, 2026

The repeated strikes also raise questions about whether Saudi Arabia has enough interceptors to sustain its defences during a prolonged campaign.

The interceptor problem

Saudi Arabia's interceptor stockpiles may have been depleted following sustained use during the wider regional conflict with Iran. Repeated missile and drone attacks can rapidly consume the expensive interceptors needed to stop incoming threats.

The United States has also expended significant quantities of Patriot and Thaad interceptors during the conflict, putting pressure on supplies that could take years to replenish.

Borsari described interceptor depletion as a "credible explanation" for the breaches, although he cautioned against treating it as the only possible cause. He pointed to media reports from last month suggesting that Riyadh was running low on ballistic missile interceptors.

"If true, this would create difficult operational trade-offs for air-defense commanders when deciding which threats to engage, how many interceptors to allocate, etc," he said. "These decisions become even more problematic during mass salvos."

The Houthis could also be attempting to saturate Saudi defenses by launching different types of weapons simultaneously, including one-way attack drones, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles. Even sophisticated, multilayered air-defense systems cannot guarantee that every incoming projectile will be intercepted during a sustained bombardment.

Borsari said it would be "naive to deny" that the Riyadh strikes raise "serious questions" about the effectiveness of Saudi Arabia’s ballistic missile defences, particularly their ability to protect fixed, high-value targets under repeated attack.

Khoueiry similarly argued that the strikes were less evidence of "a fundamental deficiency" in Saudi air defences than a reminder of the limitations facing even advanced systems. "Saudi Arabia has to defend a very large territory and prioritize coverage around major cities, military sites and critical infrastructure, while interceptor availability is also under pressure," he said. "Direct ballistic-missile impacts could reflect those constraints, but on their own they do not prove a severe interceptor shortage."

A costly game of adaptation

"We don't know what the specific cause of this failure is," Borsari said of the attacks. He noted that an air defense network's effectiveness depends on several components. "The effectiveness of a defensive network depends not simply on the sophistication of its interceptors but also on sensor coverage and integration, proficient C2 (command and control), ammunition availability, etc. So it could be any of these, or - most likely - a combination thereof."

Saudi Arabia's geography compounds those challenges. Its airports, oil facilities, ports and military installations are spread across a vast area, making continuous protection expensive and difficult to sustain.

"The main challenge is detection, and for that you need to rely on various assets, including aircraft, to ensure proper early warning," Borsari said. "But maintaining such a detection regime over time is very costly and a sustainment burden on both the equipment and personnel."

There are cheaper options for countering drones in particular, including automated anti-drone turrets equipped with heavy machine guns and low-cost short-range interceptors. But these require supporting infrastructure and careful integration with existing systems.

"So I'm afraid we will continue to see drones penetrating Saudi territory for the foreseeable future," Borsari said.

Khoueiry sees the latest Houthi strikes, alongside recent Iranian attacks on American and regional targets, as evidence of a wider effort to adapt to sophisticated air-defense systems rather than simply a matter of luck. "Iran and its partners appear to be learning how to operate against layered air defense networks, adapting flight routes and tactics to improve penetration and impose higher interception and economic costs," he said.

"The lesson for Saudi Arabia and the wider region is that increasingly sophisticated air defenses still need dense surveillance, sufficient interceptor stocks and constant adaptation to keep pace with evolving missile and drone threats."

title: A Horror Movie List To Get You In The Mood For Spooky Season
desc:
A Horror Movie List To Get You In The Mood For Spooky Season

The horror entertainment genre is a lot like comedy - Both require deep immersion and instinctive reactions. Being browbeaten with overt political messaging in the middle of such films ruins them completely. Nobody wants to hear a feminist sermon in the middle of Texas Chainsaw Massacre, they just want to watch that messed up dinner table scene.

Parable and subtle messaging is fine, but propaganda is not.

With Hollywood slowly but surely sinking into a shallow grave with little hope of escape, the industry has desperately turned to the old mainstay of horror to save the box office. Why? Because it's cheap, fast and thrives on the imagination of indie auteurs willing to engage in risky storytelling. In a world of endless remakes, reboots and "re-imaginings", audiences are desperate for something original.

And, as long as that original film isn't disgustingly ripe with leftist propaganda, everyone is generally happy.

There's not enough new and good horror productions to fill out this list of spooky season primers, but there's a few, along with some lesser known classics to get in the mood for Halloween. Let's start with the best new horror media...

Obsession

One of the biggest surprise hits of the year, Obsession follows the ill fated efforts of Baron Baily to gain the attention of his attractive co-worker Nikki Freeman. His inability to escape the "friend zone" leads him to a cursed novelty item called the "One Wish Willow". His innocent wish for Nikki to fall in love with him results in her darkly hilarious (but ultimately grotesque and disturbing) obsession with him.

The film has the obvious "careful what you wish for" horror narrative, but it gets a lot more complicated. The story stands as a perfect allegory for Gen Z men's fears over "MeToo" and the feminist culture of accusation, without ever mentioning the issue or the politics. It explores the idea of romance vs infatuation and control.

Finally, it depicts a subject matter which is rarely ever portrayed on film anymore; the weakness of beta men and their refusal to break with toxic women because they are terrified over the stigma of being alone more than the ticking time bomb that is their relationship. Like many of the films on this list, there's a element of tragic humor to this movie that sets it apart from the more lazy nihilist stories that have flooded the horror genre lately.

Widow's Bay

It's a streaming series and not a movie, but a perfect watch for the month of October. Widow's Bay is one of the few Apple TV productions actually worth a damn and one can only hope that it gets a second season despite being buried on that lifeless platform.

The series focuses on Mayor Tom Loftis, a struggling middle-aged widower trying to take care of his petulant and sometimes sociopathic teenage son in an island community oppressed by superstitious fears. It is said that anyone born on the island will die if they try to leave. The island will not let them escape.

Tom was not born on the island and doesn't believe that the place is cursed, so he attempts to rebrand Widow's Bay as a tourist destination similar to Martha's Vineyard. Hilarity and horror ensues.

The show is a mix between Parks And Recreation and The X Files with various homages to the classic horror movies of the 1980s and 1990s. It is also one of the funniest series produced in a long time, while still being extremely effective at building up supernatural dread. Each episode acts as a self contained horror tale, but the through-line plot holds together perfectly. All the characters on the island are fantastically written and fantastically weird, and the series climax is a compelling cliffhanger.

Buddy

It's strange to admit it, but this low budget parody of the 1990s "Barney" kids show might just be one of the best and most disturbing horror movies of the past decade.

Buddy is another film that is simultaneously funny and uncomfortable, you're not sure whether you're supposed to laugh or pull back in revulsion as the classic kids show filled with puppets, dancing and singing descends into a nightmare world where the children are in danger of being murdered by a rampaging homicidal supernatural unicorn.

This one is for horror fans who love to step outside of their comfort zone and it's definitely not a family film. The story plays with idea of the thin veil of reality far more effectively than the "Backrooms" flick, and gets so weird you have to admire the level of imagination it took to devise the blood curdling events that unfold.

One is immediately reminded of Peter Jackson (director of Lord Of The Rings) and his early films like "Dead Alive" and "Bad Taste". But most of all, Buddy seems to take a lot from Jackson's film "Meet The Feebles", a disturbing satire of Sesame Street and the Muppet Show in which a bunch of innocent show tunes puppets engage in increasingly depraved situations. There is also an element of the YouTube series "Don't Hug Me I'm Scared" - If you know, you know.

Oddity

Not exactly a brand new film (produced in 2024), but this movie fell by the wayside in the midst of a politically contentious year when it should have gotten more attention. This Irish horror flick is absolutely chilling, combining a murder mystery with a ghost story.

A well-to-do woman is brutally murdered while refurbishing an old estate in the Irish countryside. Her twin sister who has clairvoyant abilities, Darcy Odello, travels to the property to uncover the facts behind the case. She also carries with her a creepy wooden mannequin.

The build-up in this movie is expertly crafted and every element of it screams Halloween.

Older And Lesser Known Classics

If you're tired of watching the same standard Halloween movies every year, here are some ideas to spice up your spooky season watch list...

The Innocents

A more obscure but well loved cult classic; The Innocents is a beautifully filmed black-and-white gothic ghost tale produced in 1961 about a Governess (Miss Giddens) hired by a wealthy patron to watch over two orphaned children who seem normal at first, but start to act very strangely.

Like most supernatural movies of this time period, the story is a slow burn with creepy atmosphere. The horror comes from the ambiguity and the audience not knowing if what the main character is experiencing is real. Is Miss Giddens seeing ghosts? Are the children possessed? Or, is she losing her sanity?

In The Mouth Of Madness

A cult classic that is getting a lot more attention in recent years, John Carpenter's "In The Mouth Of Madness" is a lot like his film "The Thing". Audiences just didn't understand the genius of it at the time. It took a few decades before people were finally ready.

The movie is an homage to the interdimensional horror of H.P. Lovecraft which asks: What if our world was nothing more than a thin barrier between humanity and a dark realm where creatures older than time reside, waiting to break through and devour everything? What if, through our own bungling, we ended up tearing a hole into that terrible place?

In The Mouth If Madness has all the dark humor Carpenter is known for along with a more unfamiliar foray into cosmic horror.

Dead Alive (a.k.a Braindead)

Before Peter Jackson went down in film history for his beloved Lord Of The Rings trilogy, he was better known for making some of the weirdest and most disgusting low budget horror films of all time. The pinnacle of these films has to be "Dead Alive", also known as "Braindead".

An overzealous zoo keeper hijacks a cursed "Sumatran Rat Monkey" from forbidden tribal grounds and sends it to New Zealand, where it ends up biting the psychopathic mother of Lionel Cosgrove. The poor guy is already held hostage by the overbearing old woman and she sabotages him every time he meets a nice girl. But now, she's turning into some kind of undead creature, and the rest of the town will follow if he doesn't man up and fight back.

Will his newfound love for local grocery girl Paquita Sanchez help him to defeat an invasion from hell?

This movie is an unbelievable gore fest and for strong stomachs only. Also famous for the line: "I kick ass for the Lord!"

The Blob (1988 Remake)

Another gore fest, but with more traditional storytelling, is a remake of the 1958 classic starring Steve McQueen. This version is far more frightening and the incredible practical effects make you long for the days before everything was lazy and CG.

A rebellious small town teen (Brian Flagg) must use his cunning to stop the invasion of a formless gooey invader that uses acid to envelop and digest every living thing it touches. He also has to contend with a government agency that might not have the best interests of the town in mind.

The Witches

Based on Roald Dahl's dark fantasy novel, "The Witches" (1990 version) follows Luke, a young boy who lost his parents in a terrible accident. Luke goes to live with his eccentric but loving grandmother (Helga) who tells him scary stories about the hidden world of witches. Unlike the more innocuous and cartoonish characters of popular fiction, Helga warns Luke that witches are, in fact, real, and they are murderous monsters who prey on children.

When Luke and his Grandmother travel to a seaside hotel, Luke realizes that his grandmother was right - The resort is infested with hideous witches disguised as normal women, and they're hatching an evil plot to kill thousands of innocent kids. Unfortunately, they turn him into a mouse before he can warn anyone.

Anyone who grew up in the 1980s and early 1990s probably remembers this film, but it has faded as a Halloween classic in recent years. Perhaps because it is a family film, but like many kids movies of the era, it doesn't pull any punches with the scares. The concept of a boy and his grandmother hunting down evil witches is by itself worth a watch.

title: The Future Of American Drone Warfare
desc:
The Future Of American Drone Warfare

Authored by Adam Sharp via The Daily Reckoning,

While the war with Iran might be nearing a resolution, the war in Ukraine is heating up.

Whether this is the next stage in escalation, or the grand finale remains unclear. But lessons continue to emerge from this conflict, and world powers are beginning to act on them at scale.

Ukrainian long-range drones continue to hammer Russian energy and military sites. Targets up to 1,700 kilometers inside Russia are being hit.

A Ukrainian long-range drone. Source: AP

These strikes are causing serious economic damage to Russia, not to mention the environmental harm. Here's a screenshot of recent fires at Russia's Rosneft facility on the Black Sea after Ukrainian drone attacks.

Source: X

Earlier this week, President Trump expressed his anger at Ukrainian President Zelensky, "It's time for Ukraine to get a NEW PRESIDENT!"

Ukraine's strikes are hammering Russia's fuel production, and causing shortages worldwide.

On the front lines, short-range drones are now Ukraine's primary weapon holding back Russian advances. Most of these are small drones with anti-tank RPG warheads attached.

Crude, but highly effective. There are also bomber drones which drop grenades, mortars, and improvised munitions. Interceptor drones roam the skies, looking to foil enemy attacks.

Both sides are using flamethrower drones, which drip molten thermite to melt anti-drone netting and ignite enemy structures.

Meanwhile Russian long-range drones and missiles are increasingly hitting military sites in the capital, Kiev (Kyiv). And across the rest of the country. Glide bombs are devastating the front lines. And Russia is using at least as many short-range drones as Ukraine is.

It is estimated that up to 15,000 drones are being used in Ukraine per day. And that up to 90% of casualties are caused by these terrible little machines.

Traditional maneuver warfare is extremely difficult in these conditions. Advances crawl forward at a snail's pace.

Tanks and IFVs are increasingly irrelevant on the battlefield. Even artillery, the "God of War", has become an afterthought.

In just a few short years, this new class of drones have changed warfare forever. The question is: are American defense contractors ready for this new world?

Petraeus' Warning

Former Army General and CIA Director David Petraeus is out with a new warning about drone warfare. I'm not a fan of the man, but what he says here is true.

"We have not remotely learned all the lessons we should have from the war in Ukraine.

That is the future of war right now. Ukraine is using 10,000 drones a day.

Ninety percent of the casualties on the Russian side are caused by drones. Tanks can't manoeuvre anymore. They can't survive. Armored vehicles can't survive.

And by the way, there's more coming. Within a year or two, we're going to see unmanned systems that are not remotely piloted.

In the future, we're going to see autonomous systems - truly autonomous - that do not require a pilot to remotely operate them.

Then you face drone swarms. And that is something for which we really don't have a solution."

Weapons Giants Fall Behind

America's largest defense contractors, Lockheed Martin (LMT) and Northrop Grumman (NOC), have traditionally focused on gigantic programs. The F-35, naval ships, helicopters, cruise missiles, and big drones costing $30-90 million a piece.

These contractors have been forced to build their supply chains and manufacturing around getting support from specific political districts.

Elon Musk has been especially critical of U.S. defense firms, singling out manned fighter jets like the F-35 as "obsolete in the age of drones."

Source: X

I'm not sure fighter jets are obsolete just yet. But tanks and other traditional weapons systems do seem to be moving in that direction.

The point is that making cheap disposable "kamikaze" drones at scale is outside the wheelhouse of big defense firms.

Now that the U.S. military wants low-cost attack drones, they are doing something unusual: going to smaller firms in search of innovation.

New Drone Depots

The U.S. military is converting 6 Army depots into drone production facilities across the country. Defense Post:

The McAlester Army Ammunition Plant (MCAAP) in Oklahoma is adapting its munitions production to support modern drone warfare through a new partnership with Perennial Autonomy.

They're partnering with various private companies to build drone manufacturing capabilities domestically. Beefing up our drone production base is key to modernizing the military.

Especially because the government's requirements call for doing it without any Chinese parts.

That in itself is a huge challenge, because today China makes about 85% of the world's commercial and personal drones. China's supply chains are already incredibly developed, and it will take time to build out our own. The vast majority of Ukrainian and Russian drones used are either Chinese, or built with Chinese motors, batteries, servos, and other parts.

The Drone Dominance Program

It's been nearly 5 years since the war in Ukraine began, and the disruptive potential of drone warfare became clear.

The U.S. Department of War is now beginning to ramp up drone programs. In Iran we saw the debut of the LUCAS attack drone, based on Iran's Shahed-136.

Now the American military is looking to build 300,000 attack drones by 2028. That may sound like a lot, but it's 15 days of supply for Russia and Ukraine.

The Drone Dominance Program (DDP) is a fascinating development. The Department of War is tearing up the old playbook of 10-30 year development cycles and trying something fresh.

Dozens of companies were invited to participate in a series of trials. Various drones are tested for accuracy, speed, resistance to electronic warfare, and other objectives.

And the Department of War has an online leaderboard showing the top performers:

Source: Drone Dominance official site

Note the complete absence of any big defense contractors. The leading performer, Skycutter, is a small private U.K. company with plenty of frontline experience in Ukraine.

We are early in this new age of drone warfare. But it is set to shake up America's stale defense contracting business. New players are emerging.

The legacy defense giants have been slow to adapt to this reality. They remain focused on cash cow programs.

And for a while, that playbook will work. But the future of warfare looks like it will be dominated by unmanned systems. And the big, slow, expensive drones they make today are clearly not cut out for this new world.

American defense giants have coasted for decades on gold-plated billion-dollar contracts. They have failed to produce effective hypersonic missiles and affordable attack drones. Their reign won't last forever.

I'll be watching to see which companies emerge as leaders in this new tech. Many of them are private startups at this point, so aren't investable (yet).

But disruption is finally coming to the defense industry. It's about time.

title: "We have A Zero-Tolerance Policy": High School Student "Punished" For Expressing Support For The 'Cornell 7'
desc:
"We have A Zero-Tolerance Policy": High School Student "Punished" For Expressing Support For The 'Cornell 7'

Authored by Jonathan Turley via JonathanTurley.org,

We have previously discussed high school administrators and teachers who engage in censorship and speech regulation, often targeting religious and conservative students. These cases cost school districts millions in court costs, but the school officials never seem to face any consequences. In California, Piner High School has joined this ignoble effort, punishing the high school football captain for expressing support for the "Cornell 7" on his own Instagram page. Other students then protested not to support free speech but to demand further punishment for the student. I wonder where they learned that repressive view of free speech?

According to media reports, the unnamed student wrote "Free the Cornell Seven" on his personal Instagram account and the school called him out. As should be obvious to any teacher or administrator, this is entirely protected speech under the First Amendment. The student was not discussing the school, calling for some school disruption or destruction of property, or encouraging violence. He was stating his view that defendants who have not been tried, let alone convicted, are innocent.

This case has divided the country with many politicians and pundits declaring the guilt of these students before any charges are actually filed against them. A prosecutor previously declined to take the case to a grand jury due to conflict statements from the alleged victim.

Rather than acknowledge the serious free speech concerns raised by the school's reported actions, Santa Rosa City school's public information officer, Patrick Gannon, issued a virtue-signaling statement on how it will not tolerate students expressing such thoughts on their personal social media accounts, or presumably publicly in their private time:

"Action was taken by the school and the district, and we're continuing to have conversations. We don't tolerate making light of sexual assault. That's why we have a zero-tolerance policy."

Whatever success the school has had on basic subjects like English and Math, it has clearly taught the student body to disregard the free speech of others. The football team reportedly forfeited a game after 200 students walked out to the "Santa Rosa City Schools district offices to demand accountability and greater support for students speaking out against sexual violence."

There was no statement from Principal Andrea Correia or the school denying the reported punishment. Instead, Gannon met with the 200 students and, instead of discussing the importance of free speech and due process, said the school "wants them to know that accountability and safety are top priorities."

Students are demanding further punishment of the student for expressing his views on the case. Obviously, if the same students had posted "Justice for Jane Doe at Cornell" he would have been celebrated rather than punished.

In 1969, the Supreme Court famously declared that students do not "shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate." However, since that iconic case, federal courts have often given short shrift to the free speech rights of students.

As we have previously discussed, teachers around the country have become notorious as speech commissars who bar expressions deemed divisive or intolerant. That often includes any conservative or religious speech.

An elementary school in Kansas came under fire after Arbor Creek Elementary Principal Melissa Snell stopped the wearing of shirts reading "Freedom," which became popular after the assassination of Charlie Kirk.

In another case, U.S. District Court Judge Christopher Boyko ruled in Ohio that students could be barred from wearing "Let's Go Brandon" shirts - a coded political expression criticizing the media and former President Joe Biden. Other courts have also upheld such censorship by teachers, who claim that the expression is a substitute for a vulgar expression chanted by crowds ("F- Joe Biden"). But these shirts do not contain vulgarity. Rather, the expression is used as a defiant reference to the media bias that led to the original substitution of the words, allegedly to protect Biden - it is a "Yankee Doodling" of the political and media establishment.

Judge Karen Nelson Moore joined Sixth Circuit Judge John Nalbandian in a deeply flawed holding that, under the "vulgarity exception," the action was constitutional. The Supreme Court was asked to hear the "Let's Go Brandon" case, but recently declined to hear the case. It was a very disappointing denial from the Court for many of us in the free speech community.

In the California case, the underlying law is clear. Any punishment of this student would be a glaring violation of the First Amendment. The student can go to court to have any such actions set aside. However, it is equally clear that the administrators and teachers responsible for such actions will face no accountability.

The "zero tolerance policy" at Piner High School appears to refer to the exercise of free speech by those with unpopular or minority viewpoints. It is certainly a preview of higher education, where viewpoint intolerance and ideological orthodoxy are the norm. This chilling lesson has clearly taken hold at Piner High School.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the New York Times best-selling author of "Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution."

title: Trump DOJ Opens Civil Rights Probe Into Liberal New Jersey Town Over Gun Permit Delays
desc:
Trump DOJ Opens Civil Rights Probe Into Liberal New Jersey Town Over Gun Permit Delays

The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division has opened an investigation into the city of Pennsauken, New Jersey, on Wednesday to determine whether the township police department's handling of firearm permits has become so slow that it violates the Second Amendment.

Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon said the division's Second Amendment Section would "defend law-abiding citizens from local authorities who infringe on the right to safely carry legal firearms." She added: "Our investigation aims to discover if allegations of unconstitutional delays in firearm permitting are true, and if so, to fix it." In a statement to the Daily Caller, the DOJ said "individuals and groups" had alleged "extensive delays" in handgun purchase permits and that it had "not reached any conclusions."

The township's website lists the steps for a handgun permit to purchase: two references from outside the applicant's household, a fingerprint appointment within 90 days of applying, and a $25 fee per handgun on top of a $50 firearms purchaser ID card. The page states no processing time. Concealed carry is a separate application that asks for four references.

While the DOJ release doesn't name names, federal lawsuit filed in June 2024 fingers Pennsauken's police chief over handgun permit delays. Christian Benton, the Coalition of New Jersey Firearm Owners, Gun Owners of America and the Gun Owners Foundation filed the federal suit (No. 24-cv-7098) on June 18, 2024, challenging New Jersey's permit system and its one-handgun-a-month limit. Bearing Arms reports that Benton alleges the department took more than four months on two applications, against a 30-day state deadline, and that the case awaits summary-judgment rulings.

The legal hook is a footnote in the Supreme Court's 2022 Bruen opinion. Justice Clarence Thomas wrote that the Court did not rule out "constitutional challenges to shall-issue regimes where, for example, lengthy wait times in processing license applications or exorbitant fees deny ordinary citizens their right to public carry."

The specific type of investigation the DOJ is conducting - 'pattern-or-practice' - comes from a 1994 crime bill provision that the division has historically aimed at police misconduct. The Second Amendment Section, created inside the division in 2025, now applies it to gun permits. Brady, the gun-control group, has called that a diversion of scarce resources from traditional discrimination cases.

Los Angeles County offers a comparison. The DOJ opened a probe of the sheriff's department in March 2025, when the department said it faced "a significant staffing crisis" with 14 people in its carry-permit unit, and sued that September. The two sides settled on August 13, 2026, after the department added staff and software. DOJ says it now meets state deadlines. DOJ's complaint said applicants waited an average of 281 days, more than nine months, just for processing to begin; the sheriff disputed those figures.

Philadelphia, across the Delaware River from Pennsauken, drew a probe in June. DOJ is examining the city's police department over permit revocations that it called based on "vague" reasons. The mayor's office, the city Law Department and the police department all declined to comment to WHYY.

The section also sued San Jose in September over a roughly $1,600 permit fee and a required psychological exam. Dhillon posted about the case in September:

The @CivilRights Division sued San Jose for charging a $1,600 application fee & requiring a psych exam for a concealed carry permit. These are unconstitutional barriers and @theJusticeDept will continue to pursue cities and states blocking this right! pic.twitter.com/NGWQUj0gMN

— AAGHarmeetDhillon (@AAGDhillon) September 23, 2026

Residents who believe they were affected can file complaints online.

title: NYC Sanctuary Laws Survive As Judge Rules Feds Can't Force City To Help ICE
desc:
NYC Sanctuary Laws Survive As Judge Rules Feds Can't Force City To Help ICE

Authored by Aldgra Fredly via The Epoch Times,

A federal judge on Oct. 15 dismissed the federal government's lawsuit challenging New York City's sanctuary policy, saying that states are not obligated to participate in federal immigration enforcement.

The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) sued New York City in July 2025, alleging that its sanctuary policy was unconstitutional and impeded the government's ability to enforce federal immigration laws.

U.S. District Judge Ramon Reyes ruled that the administration lacked legal standing to bring the case, finding that federal law does not require states to assist with federal immigration enforcement.

"The United States' preemption arguments amount to nothing more than a backdoor around the Tenth Amendment and rest on a false distinction between compelling local governments' participation in federal immigration enforcement and prohibiting local governments from dictating how their personnel and other resources may be utilized towards federal immigration enforcement," the judge said.

Reyes said that striking down the challenged provisions would restrict New York City's ability to control its agencies and personnel from engaging in federal immigration enforcement, including by expending city resources to detain people and implement inter-agency information sharing.

"All potentially in violation of state law," the judge said.

"If states cannot remain free to control their agencies and employees to resist federal immigration enforcement, which is within states' constitutional prerogatives, the Tenth Amendment anticommandeering doctrine means nothing."

In a statement, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani hailed the judge's decision as "a victory for New Yorkers" and pledged to uphold the city's sanctuary laws.

"Our local laws make New York City safer. They allow us to focus our resources on protecting and serving our communities and ensuring that every New Yorker can turn to their city government without fear that asking for help will make them a target for deportation," he said.

The Epoch Times reached out to the DOJ for comment but did not receive a response by publication time.

The DOJ argued in its lawsuit that the city's sanctuary laws made it difficult for federal authorities to enforce immigration laws by preventing local officials from sharing immigrants' information such as release dates, court appearance dates, and custodial status.

"The challenged provisions also impair federal detention of removable aliens, including dangerous criminals, contrary to federal law," the complaint reads.

The suit cited the July 2025 case of an off-duty Customs and Border Protection officer who was shot by two illegal immigrants while he sat in Fort Washington Park.

The DOJ alleged that one of the immigrants had been arrested in April 2024 for felony grand larceny and petit larceny but was released after the New York City Department of Correction ignored a detainer.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said on Oct. 9 that New York City had failed to honor 14,916 immigration detainers issued by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) between Jan. 20, 2025, and Sept. 14, 2026.

The detainers were linked to 47,750 criminal charges and convictions, including homicides, sexual assaults, drug offenses, kidnapping, weapons offenses, and assaults, the department said.

The DHS statement was issued in the context of the recent shooting of Oscar Bengal, a criminal illegal immigrant in New York.

Bengal, from the Dominican Republic, was shot on Oct. 8 while federal immigration agents were attempting to arrest him in the Bronx.

Bengal was sent to a local hospital for treatment and subsequently placed in detention.

Naveen Athrappully contributed to this report.

title: "Whore Reporting For Duty": Former SNL Actress Ego Nwodim Taunts Shane Gillis After SNL Monologue
desc:
"Whore Reporting For Duty": Former SNL Actress Ego Nwodim Taunts Shane Gillis After SNL Monologue

Shane Gillis is facing criticism from several former “Saturday Night Live” performers after a joke about women's workout clothes during his latest appearance as host drew accusations of sexism, according to NBC News.

The comedian used part of his seven-minute opening monologue to poke fun at increasingly revealing gym attire, particularly the brightly colored, tight-fitting shorts worn by some women. Gillis joked that he hadn't realized women were now dressing like “whores” to exercise, before riffing on the awkwardness of men being expected not to look.

The remarks quickly circulated online, drawing criticism from viewers who accused Gillis of making unnecessary and degrading comments about women.

NBC News noted that among those responding was actor Dan Levy, who posted an Instagram video arguing that women's clothing wasn't the issue. Instead, he suggested that men who use derogatory language to describe women based on their appearance are demonstrating misogyny.

Former “SNL” cast member Cecily Strong also weighed in, posting a photo of her colorful Pilates footwear and sarcastically describing her outfit as sexually provocative. She accompanied the joke with a reference to sexual assault allegations at Cornell University, a case that has attracted attention amid the broader debate.

She wrote: “On my way to Pilates in my new slutty ass orange shoes and rainbow socks. Might sell sex on the way not sure.”

Ego Nwodim, who spent seven seasons on “SNL” before departing in 2025, offered her own response through Instagram Stories. Sharing a photo of herself dressed for the gym in black athletic clothing, she jokingly announced, “Whore reporting for duty.”

She continued the satire in a subsequent post featuring her post-workout food, making another joke about her supposed promiscuity while discussing her protein intake.

The backlash comes during Gillis' third stint hosting the NBC sketch comedy program. His relationship with the show has been controversial since 2019, when he was announced as a new cast member but dismissed shortly afterward following the resurfacing of offensive remarks from his podcast.

Despite that early controversy, Gillis has since built a successful stand-up career and returned to the program multiple times as a guest host. His latest appearance has once again put his deliberately provocative style of comedy at the center of an online debate over the boundaries of humor.

title: Negative Political Ads: Voters Despise Them, But Campaigns Keep Using Them
desc:
Negative Political Ads: Voters Despise Them, But Campaigns Keep Using Them

Authored by Russ Jones via The Epoch Times,

Campaign season has arrived with its usual barrage of attack ads, and this cycle is no exception.

Polls consistently show voters say they dislike negative advertising, yet campaigns across the country keep pouring money into it.

Political scientists, strategists and marketing experts say the answer lies in a mix of high stakes, economic anxiety, simple human psychology, and now, artificial intelligence.

A Pew Research Center survey conducted after the 2024 election found that 74 percent of voters said the campaign was "too negative," a figure that held steady from a nearly identical result in an October pre-election survey.

Travis Ridout, a political science professor at Washington State University and codirector of the Wesleyan Media Project - which tracks political advertising nationwide - said he was struck this cycle by how much of the earliest negativity came from intra-party primary fights.

"There were a lot of races where there was a lot of negativity," Ridout told The Epoch Times. "This candidate is actually a closet liberal, or this one doesn't support Donald Trump sufficiently. That sort of thing."

That dynamic defined the Texas Senate primary, where Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee and Texas attorney general, defeated incumbent Sen. John Cornyn before facing Democrat James Talarico in the general election.

Since President Donald Trump reiterated his support for Paxton's campaign in late August, more than $100 million in mostly negative ads targeting Talarico has poured in from GOP-aligned political committees, including the Senate Leadership Fund, which alone spent nearly $66 million in September. These funds have contributed to ads accusing Talarico of being a "radical liberal" and an "extremist."

"The Texas Senate race is certainly standing out, just because the negativity started so early. ... A lot of it is focused on DEI or those sorts of things, so the more cultural issues," Ridout said.

Talarico, a state representative who has out-raised Paxton but said he received little outside help from national Democratic groups, said "dark money super PACs are flooding the airwaves with lies about me and my record," at a rally at Baylor University in Waco.

Talarico has also aired ads labeling Paxton "the most corrupt politician in Texas," highlighting Paxton's 2023 impeachment by the Texas House. Paxton was later acquitted by the state Senate.

The pattern extends beyond Texas.

In Georgia and North Carolina, the Senate Leadership Fund has aired ads attacking Democratic candidates, including Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia, over transgender rights, reviving a line of attack from 2024.

The California governor's race has produced a new kind of attack ad. Republican Steve Hilton's campaign has aired AI-generated videos portraying Democrat Xavier Becerra as a puppet and associating him with what the campaign calls the "Democratic machine."

Meanwhile, Becerra's campaign has relied mainly on public statements to frame Hilton as Trump's "lapdog" and accuse Hilton of welcoming immigration enforcement "mercenaries" into California.

In Ohio, a series of political spots connects Republican state Sen. Jon Husted to a bribery scandal and the passage of House Bill 6, the controversial 2019 statute that authorized a $1 billion bailout for two nuclear power plants. State investigative records and federal court filings indicate that Husted has never been indicted, criminally charged, or formally accused of wrongdoing by law enforcement.

A parallel ad campaign in Maine by the Democratic super PAC WinSenate launched a $3.4 million advertising blitz focusing on "pay-to-play" allegations against Republican Sen. Susan Collins and a former defense contractor. Collins has issued explicit denials regarding any such schemes, and an FBI spokesperson told reporters that the agency's initial inquiry yielded no evidence implicating Collins or her campaign.

Why Campaigns Go Negative

Jay Revell, an adjunct instructor in Florida State University's Master's in Applied American Politics and Policy program and owner of the public relations firm Revell Media, shared with The Epoch Times that the stakes explain much of the surge.

"The higher the stakes, the more likely you are to see a lot of negative attacks," he said.

With control of Congress on the line, he said that dynamic is playing out from the top of the ballot to local races.

Ridout pointed to psychology.

"There's good psychology in support of a negativity bias, so people might be paying more attention when something's negative," he said.

"Part of it, especially, is to define one's opponent, to draw a contrast. You've got to create that contrast, and one way to do that is through campaign negativity."

Revell said this cycle is also shaped by economic pressure.

Rising prices, including at the gas pump, have widened the gap between voters who are struggling and those who are not, he said, giving challengers an opening to blame incumbents directly.

"There's just so much fodder out there in the world, based in truth and reality about the scenarios that people are facing, that you're seeing a lot more negative attacks pointing the blame at people versus just broad negative attacks about who they are," he said.

He said ads that draw a clear line between a policy and a voter's daily experience tend to resonate more than ones that simply declare a candidate a "bad person."

"There needs to be a one-to-one relationship with the truth for a message to be effective," Revell said.

"People need to hear that message and feel like, yes, that connects. That feels like it's based in reality."

Does Negativity Work?

The research on negative ads is mixed, Ridout said. "The best answer political scientists have right now is they work sometimes," he said.

"On average, they probably work as well as positive ads, but it depends on the context and the stage of the campaign."

Timing matters too, he said.

Negative ads can help define an opponent early, before voters form lasting impressions, but the tactic carries risk.

"There's a risk of a backlash," he said. "People won't like that negativity, and they'll take it out against the sponsor."

Speaking with The Epoch Times from Plano, Texas, Sheila Rondeau, a marketing strategist and CEO of MOGXP, said perception can matter more than substance.

"The prettier the person, the prettier the messaging; it seems to do better," she said.

"It seems very superficial, but it is just like artwork. It is just like labels. People pick the pretty bottle, the pretty label on the bottle of wine they choose."

Rondeau pointed to Paxton's primary as a case where negative advertising didn't decide the outcome.

He absorbed heavy attacks and still won by a wide margin over an opponent who outspent him roughly ninefold, she said.

AI Enters the Ad Wars

Ridout said this cycle also marks a leap in AI-generated content. "We've tracked about 170 different ads this season that have used AI," he said.

"That's undoubtedly an undercount."

Some are deepfakes showing a candidate saying or doing something that never happened, he said. Others are subtler, implying a candidate's presence by showing only the back of a person's head or a pant leg, or using AI to generate backdrops like a county fair or a bait shop.

"Other times they're just using AI more as a tool for video editing," he said.

That uncertainty is exactly what worries Mark Grebner, a Michigan-based political consultant who has run campaigns since 1973 and been elected 25 times as a county commissioner.

He said most negative advertising this cycle, including ads targeting Michigan congressional candidates Abdul El-Sayed and Will Lawrence, has become so generic that he suspects some of it is not written by people at all.

"It would not surprise me if this dreadful level, this soup of negativism, comes out of an AI generator," he told The Epoch Times. "It has all the feeling of third-rate thinking, not quite right, stock character."

Interchangeable Attacks

"I kind of think that we've gotten to the point that it's just like the weather or something," Grebner said. "You can complain about it, and you can pay attention if you want, but it's just endless and unavoidable. So I think that the average person isn't really affected anymore."

He said the messaging is nearly indistinguishable from race to race.

"It's all the same thing. It doesn't really have anything particularly to do with the candidates. It's just the word "dangerous," "socialist," "frightening," and "un-American," he said.

"Negative campaigning, in order to work, has to actually tell you something new about a person that you can kind of apply to them."

By contrast, he said the most effective negative ad he ever ran, decades ago, worked because it was specific. He mailed an opponent's own attack, that Grebner wasn't a 22-year-old student anymore - like his opponent - to the older, non-student voters in his district, quietly reminding them he was, in fact, an adult homeowner.

"That was devastating to his campaign," he said, adding that a version of the mailer was later reprinted in Harper's magazine.

Grebner cited informal estimates suggesting it can take roughly a million ad exposures to shift a single vote. "I can believe that," he said. "I think that's the experiment we're doing."

AdImpact projected total political ad spending for 2025-2026 at $11.6 billion, the most of any election cycle on record.

AdImpact data show a sharp partisan divide in political advertising during the first half of October. Republicans devoted 80 percent of their ad spending to negative ads and the remaining 20 percent to contrast ads, with none classified as positive. Their messaging focused heavily on taxes and transgender healthcare.

Democratic advertising was more often framed as contrast. Roughly 58 percent of spending went to contrast ads, 23 percent to negative ads and 19 percent to positive ads. The October figures come amid a record-setting cycle.

Voters Keep Watching Anyway

Ridout, Revell, Rondeau, and Grebner all pointed, in different ways, to the same disconnect. What voters claim to want and how they behave rarely match.

Rondeau compared it to rubbernecking at a traffic accident.

"People say they hate them. But they listen to them, and they repeat them," she said. "It is almost like the people who are in the cars who get so angry because there is a traffic jam, but they can't stop turning to look at the ambulance."

Revell said the anonymity of many campaign donors compounds public unease.

"When you put shadows in place where the money can hide, and you don't know who's sending out messages and you don't know who's paying for it, it just adds to that anxiety," he said.

Rondeau said the cycle is unlikely to break as long as it keeps working.

"As long as people listen and share, and it gets picked up by the media, they will continue to go negative," she said.

"When we stop listening to it, and it stops working, then we will have debates about true content and character."

title: Supreme Court Leaves Self-Described Antifa Member Jailed Before Trial
desc:
Supreme Court Leaves Self-Described Antifa Member Jailed Before Trial

The Supreme Court this week turned down an emergency request to let Kyle Wagner, a 37-year-old self-described Antifa member from Minneapolis, out of jail before his trial. Wagner is charged in federal court in Michigan with one count of cyberstalking and one count of transmitting interstate threats.

Both counts stem from his dealings with a man identified in court documents as J.S., a pro-ICE social media figure. Prosecutors say that on Jan. 29 Wagner doxxed J.S. - posting his name, phone number and address, along with what he believed were his parents' details, and wrote, "we can all knock on strangers doors." According to the Solicitor General's filing opposing release, which quotes the Sixth Circuit's account of the record, the posts around it were far broader: he declared that Minneapolis was "kill or be killed," told followers to "hunt" ICE and lamented that protesters had not marched on the Whipple federal building "with guns." The same account says he raised between $10,000 and $15,000 from followers to help him evade detection, and that Instagram deleted his account before he resurfaced under a new handle.

Wagner's lawyers say the record shows a protester, not a plotter - noting that he has no violent criminal history, owned no weapons and advocated nonviolent protest, and Courthouse News reports he offered limits on his movements and internet use. His lawyers argued he is "being detained not on the basis of a history of violence, but rather based on his speech."

A magistrate judge in Minnesota first ordered him held, citing the posts, his lack of stable work or housing and his stated desire to evade law enforcement. U.S. District Judge Denise Page Hood then revoked that order, though she acknowledged the government had made "a very strong argument" on public safety. She released him to his mother's home in Minnesota with GPS monitoring, a ban on social media posting and limits to two approved devices. On Aug. 12, a divided Sixth Circuit panel reversed her. Judges Hermandorfer and Norris held that no set of conditions would protect J.S. and the public, and Judge Bloomekatz dissented.

It gets better...

Wagner faces additional charges for conspiracy to impede or injure federal officers in a separate case. Federal prosecutors claim Wagner and others engaged in coordinated efforts to disrupt federal operations during Operation Metro Surge in the Twin Cities.

A different judge ordered Wagner to be released on those charges, however, leaving him in detention solely based on the cyberstalking case. -Courthouse News

The Sixth Circuit's own opinion, as the government's brief quotes it, gives Wagner some ground. It conceded that he has no violent criminal history, a factor it said weighed "slightly against dangerousness," and it ruled for the government anyway. The majority leaned on the threats, on his alleged willingness, in a Signal chat two days before his arrest, to entertain a request to help "kill" a former senior government official, and on a record of missed state court dates that included an "absconder" listing and an active Iowa warrant. It also held that Judge Hood's remark that public protection depends on "what side of the street you're on" had no bearing on the question. Prosecutors say Wagner shoved and spat at the arresting agents and flashed his middle fingers in his booking photo, saying it was "for the judge." Bloomekatz read the "barrel of a gun" post as describing followers being threatened, and said the Signal exchange weighed only slightly toward dangerousness.

The Supreme Court was not asked to decide whether the posts were threats. Wagner wanted a stay while the justices consider his Sept. 18 petition, which asks whether appeals courts must defer to a district judge's release decision or review it from scratch. The Solicitor General answered that this is no emergency. The government says the dispute becomes moot when trial opens Jan. 12, 2027, after Wagner himself delayed it four times. The postponements ran from April to July, September, November and now January, and the brief says he admits the aim was to keep the issue alive. It also noted the Court turned down the same standard-of-review question in 2022. The reports on Tuesday's order did not address the petition itself.

The prosecution arrived with an announcement. In a Feb. 5 statement the Epoch Times quotes, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi said the man "allegedly doxxed and called for the murder of law enforcement officers" and "proudly claimed affiliation with the terrorist organization Antifa." The Justice Department announced the arrest in a release. Courthouse News notes that Antifa is a decentralized movement with no official organization, though President Donald Trump designated it a domestic terrorist organization by executive order last year.

As we reported, that September order told agencies to investigate and dismantle the group and anyone acting on its behalf, and what we called the first Antifa terrorism case ended with five guilty pleas over an attack on a Texas detention center. The Michigan charges against Wagner are a different kind of test: they rest on what he wrote and posted online, not on an attack.

title: Things Have Changed...
desc:
Things Have Changed...

Authored by James Howard Kunstler via kunstler.com,

I remind you once again: history is a trickster. Sometimes things turn out, and sometimes they just turn, and these days they're turning hard. Get this: Russia is not our mortal enemy anymore. This is not 1956 or even 1986. It is no longer the so-called Free World against the wicked Hammer and Sickle.

Russia is no longer a weird political science experiment acting in defiance of human nature - that is, of people striving to make good lives for their families. No more sacrificing everyone's happiness to prove Karl Marx's cockamamie theories. No more trying to foist all that on the rest of the world. Russia gave up on that project and opted to become a normal nation, with the full kit of normality: commerce, shopping, banks, enterprise. Things have changed.

Things have gotten strange, too. You see every indication that, for now, Europe has become something of adversary, if not exactly our enemy, yet. Europe has lost its mind. Now, it is Europe's turn to destroy itself in pursuit of idiotic theories - such as: nations don't matter. . . you can have a high standard of living without productive industry. . . carbon is destroying the world.

Europe is now tyrannized by the unelected EU commission, much as the old Soviet Union was tyrannized by its politburo. An Orwellian switcheroo has occurred. When history plays tricks, it plays doozies. So, now you've got the grandmotherly Ursula von der Leyen dictating what all the countries in Europe may do and not do with their farms and factories and the daily lives of their people, just like Joseph Stalin in 1937. And you have the grotesquely weak leaders of France, Germany, and the rest submitting to this.

And outside the EU - which it voted to exit in 2016 - you have our so-called "mother country," Great Britain (the United Kingdom) committing suicide in the most extravagant way, turning over prime ministers like they were jacks in a game of whist, jailing their own people for impure thoughts, while allowing the wholesale rape of its womenfolk by foreign invaders. Most extraordinary, as Dr. Watson might have observed to old Sherlock. Meanwhile, they have the ragged remnant of their old empire to defend, and it's not going so well.

That remnant is all that's left of Britain's economy: its banks, its Wall Street, which they call The City of London, a square mile of hideous skyscrapers by which Britain desperately seeks to maintain financial flows into an economy that increasingly produces nothing. Which is to say, all that's left of Britain's vast imperial power is a matrix of nefarious financial rackets - just as, in the USA, all that's left of the old Democratic Party is its matrix of rackets.

These days, Britain's political apparatus is working hard to scare-up a war with Russia as a last-ditch attempt to salvage its hopelessly wasted economy. Britain's leadership apparently thinks it can summon a war economy and even draft an army of foot-soldiers as if this were 1914 or 1939. It's an insane project, based on an age-old wish to capture the vast natural resources of Russia. They've been at it, like, forever. (France and Germany tried it, too. Didn't work.)

Now we, here in the USA, in our own hemisphere of the globe, far across the salty seas from Europe, had been enlisted in this project to mess with Russia since 1991, and that's not working so well anymore, either. First of all, there is the NATO problem. We're still entangled in that anachronistic treaty, despite Russia having opted to be normal thirty-five years ago. So, you see, the way to get Russia was to stir up a war between it and Ukraine.

And they used us to do it - because the EU+ NATO lacked the mojo for the job. They got our Anglified State department and its NeoCon errand boys, along with our intel cowboys and their "Five-Eye" pardners, to stage the 2014 Maidan Revolution in Kiev, kick out the Russia-friendly president Viktor Yanukovych and, after running through a couple of puppet presidents, installed the former comedian Zelenskyy in the job (who had played a buffoonish Ukrainian president on TV previously, another great prank by our friend, history).

The next gambit was to try to shoe-horn Ukraine into NATO, which everybody knew would provoke Russia to move against Ukraine, which it did in 2022. Russia did not want NATO military bases on its border. That, Mr. Putin declared, loudly enough to be heard in Berlin, Paris, London, and Brussels, was a "red line." Voila, war! And the USA being the backbone and the bank account for NATO, got dragged into backing Ukraine by the feckless "Joe Biden" - years on Ukraine's bribery payroll, and too out-of-it to not be punked into playing along. Yeah, he said, you can join NATO. The blue and yellow flags busted out all over our land. Slava Ukraini, the useful idiots shrieked.

President Donald Trump, having survived the Ukraine phone call impeachment gambit and many other attempts to put him out of business, was wise to the game, and one of the first things he did returning to power in 2025 was to confab with Vladimir Putin in Alaska. Against all odds, Mr. Trump has maintained that working relationship despite having to pretend to support NATO. He apparently realizes that the tricks of history have placed the USA in greater alignment with Russia than with our former World War Two allies, most particularly a desire to avoid the World War Three that NATO is now pushing for.

The President has made it clear that he is done with the weaselly Zelenskyy and all his machinations - his visits to suck-up with King Charles, his nefarious dealings with NATO, his monstrous money-laundering. If Mr. Trump has not yet secretly withdrawn America's remaining support for Ukraine via NATO, he will do so soon, explicitly, and in a way that is liable to be an end to NATO, which trickster-history has managed to turn into a warmonger. The EU and NATO do not have the money to keep that war going. It's as simple as that.

Now, Iran. Americans are badly exercised by this operation, which has so far claimed around twenty lives. Well, there's an election on, and you can be sure that a lot of this discontent is being generated by 1) the desperate Democratic Party and 2) the various characters in what's being called "Woke MAGA." The peeved apostates, such as Tucker, Candace, MTG, and company, might be acting under, shall we say, foreign influence, but they also seem plumb crazy. In the case of Tucker and Candace, of course, the ideas they've been retailing seem garishly insane. Tucker babbles about literal infestations of Satan-sent demons, and sneers Goebbels-like against the Jews, while Candace follows her cuckoo Charlie Kirk vengeance project.

Get this: Iran has lost this war, and badly. And for a good reason: being that they were determined to develop nuclear weapons and long-range missiles to deliver them, and President Trump made the reasonable decision that it better not happen. Iran, being run by a lunatic Jihad faction, the IRGC, refuses to come to reasonable terms. The few weeks left before the US midterm election make this an especially delicate period. The Iranians well know this, and are playing it for all it's worth in hopes that a flip of the US Congress will improve their position. It's a bad bet.

The president has made it pretty clear, and consistently so for months. The Iranians can either agree to become a normal nation, even prosperous, happy one, but with no nukes and no more jihad, or we are going to put them out of business - whichever way the midterm election goes. In other words, what you're seeing now in that corner of the globe is not the final disposition of things.

The Europeans apparently have an incentive to do whatever they can do keep feeding the flames in Ukraine and Iran, though they are not advertising it overtly. Our interests have diverged. The Europeans are maneuvering in such a way as to make themselves an adversary to the USA, a very unwise move. It also happens that their countries are going up in flames at the moment. Their citizens are not happy, and they are further belabored by a large force of invading savages. The leaders in charge of those countries might not be in charge a whole lot longer. Think about recalibrating your expectations about where all this is going. And don't be so glum. The odds are in our country's favor, and these wars can be resolved favorably.

title: Ukraine's Starlink & Starshield Services Restored, Officials Say
desc:
Ukraine's Starlink & Starshield Services Restored, Officials Say

British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting confirmed on Oct. 15 that Ukraine's access to SpaceX's Starlink and Starshield services had been restored following a temporary disruption.

Starshield is the military version of Starlink, which offers satellite internet connectivity for consumer and commercial use.

The temporary disruptions to Ukraine's Starshield access, which were reported on Oct. 14, come amid increased tension between President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Adding more confusion to this whole scenario, around midday on Friday, President Trump told a gaggle of reporters that he "didn't know who gave the order on Starshield," to slow it down, claiming further that "it wasn't us."

President Trump says the U.S. has not restricted SpaceX’s military-grade Starshield satellite communications services to Ukraine. pic.twitter.com/K1fZNgpVRa

— Tabz (@TabzLIVE) October 16, 2026

As Timothy Frudd further reports for The Epoch Times, following a meeting with U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth on Oct. 15, Streeting told the BBC that he was "reassured directly" by Hegseth that Ukraine's access to Starlink and Starshield had been restored.

On Friday, Zelenskyy said satellite speed was returning but had not yet been fully restored to its previous levels.

Asked whether the Pentagon had restricted Ukraine's access to the satellite network to prevent strikes on Russian energy infrastructure during a Thursday interview on Fox News's "The Story with Martha MacCallum," Streeting said, "That's not my understanding."

"We didn't really get into why the service interruption had happened. We did reflect briefly on the fact that it had been restored and welcome that," he said.

Ukrainian officials said on Oct. 14 that its military access to Starshield services was temporarily restricted overnight, resulting in disruptions to combat missions.

Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy, said the restrictions impacted devices connected to Starshield's services that were moving over 100 mph.

"I confirm that SpaceX has implemented speed limits for Starlink terminals while in motion," Beskrestnov wrote in a statement on Telegram. "Our defense forces were not notified of this restriction, and it has resulted in the disruption of several missions."

Ukraine uses Starlink's satellite services to support drones used to strike Russian targets, intercept Russian drones, and for military communications.

Yevhen Karas, commander of Ukraine's 413th Separate Unmanned Systems Regiment, which specializes in drone operations, said the military lost drones due to communication disruptions and that some missions had failed.

"The Starshield shutdown was short, lasted only one day, but several drones and other systems were affected," he said.

Following reports of the disruptions by Ukrainian officials on Wednesday, Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski questioned SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, asking whether the restrictions were linked to political pressure.

Responding to the issue, Musk said the U.S. government owns and controls the Starshield systems.

"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote in an X statement.

Asked about the temporary restrictions on Ukraine's access to Starshield, a U.S. official told The Epoch Times, "No such request was ever made by the president."

The Epoch Times reached out to the Pentagon for comment but did not receive a response in time for publication.

After weeks of pushing for a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on attacks targeting energy infrastructure, Trump criticized Zelenskyy on Oct. 10 for continuing to strike Russian oil and gas refineries and suggested that it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president."

Trump's criticism came after Zelenskyy voiced opposition to a deal the Trump administration made with Russia to supply diesel to the global market.

On Oct. 11, Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an energy ceasefire.

However, Ukraine has since resumed attacks on Russian refineries after Zelenskyy said Kyiv was "done" complying with the ceasefire, accusing Russia of continuing to launch attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

In a Thursday interview on Newsmax's "Finnerty," Trump was asked about Ukraine's resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries.

Trump described Zelenskyy as "not a good guy for us to deal with," adding that he was "not a big fan" of the Ukrainian president.

Trump told Newsmax that he believes Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelenskyy both want to see the war ended and that it "should end soon."

"But I think I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult to deal with than Putin," Trump added.

title: US Closes Fiscal 2026 With $2 Trillion Budget Deficit, Pays Record $1.4 Trillion In Interest
desc:
US Closes Fiscal 2026 With $2 Trillion Budget Deficit, Pays Record $1.4 Trillion In Interest

With DOGE disbanded more than a year ago, and tariffs struck down by the Supreme Court, the US is no longer even pretending that there is any hope to normalize spending, or any kind of happy ending to the US debt trajectory.

At 2pm today the US Treasury published the latest, September, monthly budget deficit data, which was also the last month of fiscal 2026, and it will again come as no surprise to anyone that things are looking ever worse.

Total US receipts for the month were $558 billion, a modest 2.6% improvement from the $544 billion a year ago, with individual income taxes accounting for $298 billion, or more than half of the total, and the bulk of the balance coming from Social Insurance and Retirement receipts of $149 billion.

On the spending side, things were ugly: total outlays were $585 billion, a 70% deterioration from the $345.7 billion spent a year ago, although like last month, much of that had to do with the calendar impact of tariffs.

Putting receipts and spending in context, a chart of the trailing 6 months of government revenue and spending shows that the two trendlines continue to diverge with spending on pace to surpass the covid all time high, even as government revenue remains stuck in a much more narrow range.

The difference between the two, is of course, the US budget deficit, which in September was $27 billion, an improvement from August's 167 billion deficit, which however was the result of some calendar discrepancies between the two months.

It's worth noting that after several months of EPS-boosting tariff refunds (courtesy of the Supreme Court), in September the US was once again collecting net tariff revenues, if at the normal rate from before Trump's latest trade war.

What matters more is that for the full fiscal 2026, total US deficit is closed the year at $2 trillion (technically $1.992 trillion), over $200 billion worse than last year. The silver lining is that contrary to what we said a month ago, when we predicted that "2026 will be about $200bn worse than the previous year when all is said and done, and be the 3rd worst year for the US deficit on record, with just the crisis years of 2020 and 2021 worse", 2026 was actually just fractionally better than 2023 and its $2.014 trillion deficit.

Finally, turning to the elephant in the room, namely interest expense, in September the US spent $92 billion on gross interest expense, which means for all of fiscal 2026, total US interest spending has risen to a record $1.360 trillion, up 12% from a year ago, and the highest on record (as for the net vs gross nazis, in September the US for the first time ever paid net interest of more than a trillion dollars, or $1.05TN to be precise)

Extrapolating the current trend (and with the recent Fed rate hike our estimate may prove conservative), on an LTM basis, total US interest of $1.4 trillion is set to surpass Social Security (which was $1.67 trillion LTM but growing much slower), by the end of 2028.

And since 23% of marketable US debt is now T-Bills, which will see an immediate impact from the recent (and coming) Fed hikes, US interest expense is going to rise even more sharply, signaling that while the debt endgame for the US is guaranteed, the only question is whether Warsh will bring it on even faster.
