title: Bad Inflation Cures Itself. Good Inflation Doesn't
desc:
Bad Inflation Cures Itself. Good Inflation Doesn't

Authored by Lance Roberts via RealInvestmentAdvice.com,

Key Takeaways

  • Inflation driven by supply shocks is "bad" inflation, and bad inflation is self-liquidating because rising income doesn't support it.
  • September headline CPI ran 3.7% while core sat at 2.6%. The gap is gasoline, up 34.2% over the year and now more than half of the monthly increase.
  • Real wages have turned negative, and labor's share of output just set its lowest reading since the series began in 1947.
  • The 10-year breakeven sits near 2.3%. The market that gets paid to price inflation is not pricing an inflation problem.

Most of the argument about inflation right now is a fight between people using the same word for two completely different things. One side sees a 3.7% headline print and starts sketching a repeat of 1979. The other sees core running more than a point below it and declares the problem solved. Both are reading the same release. The distinction that matters is not how big the number is, but whether anybody's income is financing it. That is the line between "good" inflation and bad inflation, and almost nobody draws it.

Good Inflation, Bad Inflation, And The Difference Nobody Makes

There is a general framework to inflation, and it is older than any of us. Prices can rise because buyers are bidding for scarce goods with money they've actually earned. Or prices can rise because the cost of producing something has jumped for reasons unrelated to demand. An oil embargo will do it, as we saw in the 1970s. So does a shuttered Strait of Hormuz, a new tariff schedule, or a pandemic that takes half the world's shipping capacity offline for eighteen months.

This is an important point for the "debasement" crowd, whose narrative overlooks the underlying fundamentals.

"The following economic illustration is taught in every 'Econ 101' class. Unsurprisingly, inflation is the consequence if supply is restricted and demand increases via monetary interventions."

However, there is a very important distinction to be made about inflation. The first type is the "good" kind of inflation, and it is genuinely good. Demand pushes prices up; firms book wider margins; tight labor markets funnel those margins into paychecks, and the higher paychecks fund the higher prices. The loop closes and becomes self-reinforcing because every leg of it is paid for by real output.

The second kind, the "bad" kind of inflation, closes nothing. A tariff is a tax, just like an oil shock is a tax. Somebody's cost went up, and the money has to come out of a budget that did not grow. Every dollar of that price increase is a dollar not spent somewhere else. Bad inflation doesn't create the income that pays for it, so it destroys the demand that supports it. Such is the mechanism behind the oldest saying in commodities: "high prices cure high prices."

Think of it this way. A group of people drives the same way to work every day. Half get a raise, the other half doesn't. The city decides to put a toll booth on the road they drive to work; each year, that toll rises. Both groups have an increasing number draining their bank accounts each month. However, only one group has sufficient compensation to continue using the toll road. The group without the compensation raise is eventually forced to stop using the toll road; traffic falls, and the operator cuts the toll to win them back.

What The September Print Actually Says

Let's review the recent August data to see what the message, versus the narrative, actually is. The headline CPI came in at 3.7% year over year in September. Core came in at 2.6%, a tick higher than August. Read that pair again, because it is the whole argument. The gap between them widened from nine-tenths of a point to one and a tenth, meaning the headline accelerated roughly three times faster than the core.

That gap suggests a very different narrative than what the media suggests. Gasoline rose 9.1% in the month alone and 34.2% over the year, and the BLS attributes over half the entire monthly increase in the all-items index to that one category. Energy overall is up 20.4%. Meanwhile, core goods, where a genuine demand boom would show up first and loudest, rose 0.7% over twelve months, sitting exactly where it was in August. Shelter ticked up to 3.2%

Now the part I owe you, because I set a test in advance. Core ticked up, shelter ticked up, and services' less energy reached 3.1%, which would eventually prove me wrong. One month of tenths is noise rather than a trend. It is also the first month this year that those three moved the wrong way together, and core goods holding flat at 0.7% is why I am not moving yet, because that is where a demand boom announces itself first, and it has not.

Headline CPI pulled further away from core in September. The shaded area is the spread, and the spread is energy. Source: BLS via Massive Market Data, September 2026.

I've been making this argument since June, when I wrote about why the May 4.2% headline was an oil story rather than a demand story. To wit:

"A 4.2% headline that is three-fifths gasoline is not the same animal as a 4.2% headline driven by wages, rents, and services broadening."

Four months later, the composition has not changed. What has changed is that the evidence against the demand-pull story got considerably stronger.

Labor Just Set A 79-Year Low

The most important evidence comes from the labor market. If this were the "good" kind of inflation, workers would be capturing some of it. They are not.

Real average hourly earnings fell 0.7% over the twelve months through September, more than double the August decline. Nominal wages rose 0.1% on the month against a 0.6% CPI print, so purchasing power went backward at the fastest pace of the year. Run the same calculation off average hourly earnings and CPI, and you land in the same place. Real wage growth is near -0.7%, down from over 1.5% as recently as last spring.

In April 2026, real wage growth crossed below zero and hit its weakest reading in September. The gold bars represent the months when wages grew faster than prices. The red bars are months when they didn't. Source: BLS via Massive Market Data, August 2026.

Then there is the one number that everyone simply overlooked. In the second quarter, labor's share of nonfarm business output fell to 52.8%. The Bureau of Labor Statistics flagged that as the lowest level in a series that begins in the first quarter of 1947. Read that again. There have been 79 years of data, 2 dozen business cycles, 4 major wars, the Volcker shock, the China trade shock, and the pandemic. Despite all that, in what is supposed to be an economic boom, we just set a record low.

Labor's share of nonfarm business output in Q2 2026, the lowest reading since the series began in 1947.

Labor's share of output has been falling for a quarter century and just made a series low. Good inflation requires this line to rise. Source: BLS, Productivity and Costs, Q2 2026.

Stop and notice that in the chart above, this is not a 2026 event. The erosion in labor runs back to the early 2000s, long before "artificial intelligence" or "surging debt." The last two years have simply accelerated the numbers. With respect to the inflation question, the timing matters most. A price level that is rising while labor's slice of output hits an all-time low is the textbook signature of cost pass-through rather than demand-pull. In this environment, corporations are fixated on protecting profit margins, while workers are absorbing the difference.

The economic activity surveys tell the same story if you take the time to read past the headlines. The ISM services printed 54.9 in September, with new orders easing to 59.8. That reads like a demand boom until you see prices paid at 74.0, the highest since July 2022, against an employment index that has not managed to exceed 50.1 in three months. Steady orders, hot input costs, flat payrolls. When respondents were asked what was driving those costs, fuel came up about twice as often as anything else.

Where The Inflation Bulls Have A Point

As always, we need to examine both sides of every argument, as the inflation bulls do have a valid point.

The strongest one is the AI buildout. Memory is genuinely scarce; its scarcity is genuinely caused by capital spending, and the producer price index for storage devices has climbed 23% since the end of 2024, while import prices for computers and parts are up 37%. J.P. Morgan's research team puts the memory shock at 0.2% to 0.4% on core inflation. That is capex-driven price pressure; it is real, and it did not come from an embargo. However, that scarcity will eventually reverse. As with oil prices, high prices eventually curtail demand.

The second argument is that tariffs are a policy choice, not a weather event. That is a true statement, and a tariff regime that stays in place for years produces a price level that stays elevated for years. Calling that "transitory" is a semantic trick. I can't argue with that. A permanent tax produces a permanent price. However, the current tariffs were not enacted by Congressional legislation, which would make them more permanent. In this case, they were enacted through executive order, which means the next Administration can repeal them quickly.

The third is that energy is not reliably mean-reverting on any schedule you can trade. Geopolitics doesn't run on a calendar. However, high oil prices, as shown in the chart below, reliably mean-revert over time.

Those are all sound and valid arguments, but there is a problem with all three, though. Every one of them describes a SUPPLY constraint. A memory shortage is, by definition, a shortage. Call the tariff what it is: a tax. And the Middle East risk is a supply risk. None of them creates the income that pays the higher price. All three fail the same test: gasoline fails, and a more flattering story doesn't change what the bill does to a household budget.

Why Bad Inflation Cures Itself

"Inflation is inflation. My grocery bill doesn't care about the taxonomy."

That is a fair statement. The pain from inflation is the same either way, and when you are staring at the number on the gas pump, the squeeze on household budgets happens regardless. Just because it happens to be the academically preferable kind, the household budget just doesn't care. However, the taxonomy isn't about how it feels, but how it ends, and bad inflation ends in a way the good kind never does.

Every major energy spike since 1971 has reversed within one to two years. The 2008 spike gave way to a 25% collapse. The 2022 spike gave way to a 17% collapse. Source: BLS, CPI energy index via FRED, through September 2026.

Notably, look at what happens after every spike on that chart. In June 2008, energy jumped by more than 24%, then subsequently fell by 25% over the following year. In June 2022, energy surged by 41.5%, then only to fall by 16.6% by 2023. Every period from the 1974 and 1980 shocks, the 2000 run, and the 2015 collapse is the same. The pattern repeats itself because it has to, since "demand destruction" is not an economic theory; it's just arithmetic. The current reading of roughly 20% sits well inside the range that has always reverted.

Such is why the bond market refuses to panic. The 10-year breakeven inflation rate is 2.33% as of October 13, and the September monthly average was 2.36%. That number has barely moved all year, holding a range of roughly 2.24% to 2.44% while headline CPI swung from 2.4% up to 4.2% and back to 3.7%. The one market that gets paid to be right about inflation looked at an 180-basis-point headline swing and didn't blink. It then watched September print three-tenths hotter and tick down.

Critically, this is where the case from the "Persistent Purveyors Of Doom" gets confused with itself. Yes, bond yields are elevated, and the bears point at that as vindication for their case. The 10-year sits near 5.1% and the 30-year above 5.55%. But if you decompose it, the rise is due to real yield and the term premium, not inflation expectations, because expectations have been pinned near 2.3% for 18 months. Since early September, the long bond has added about 30 basis points, while the breakeven has given up 3. The bears are right that the long end is repricing. They just have the wrong reason.

Five tests, and five answers pointing in the same direction, which all bring to mind a rule to live by.

"When every strategist on television agrees that inflation is structural and yields only go up, the setup is usually pointed the other way."

What This Means For Portfolios

Will bad inflation cure itself on a schedule you can put in a calendar? No. Demand destruction takes quarters, not weeks, and an energy shock can persist long enough to cause real damage as it resolves. Such is the frustration of running a process that works in quarters for clients who measure in weeks. But will it resolve without the Fed having to break something? On this evidence, probably yes, and that is a very different portfolio than the one the inflation-forever crowd is selling.

It argues for duration, which is the position I laid out in my discussion about wage growth as a leading inflation indicator. Since then, the real wage data has reinforced that positioning. Investors who bought commodity-linked exposure as an inflation hedge may have the wrong trade. The reason is that commodities would hedge the one kind of inflation that has historically unwound. However, quality equities with pricing power beat the debt-heavy cyclicals that need a nominal boom to work. Most notably, watch the labor data rather than the CPI headline. Labor is where the answer lives.

In the current environment, as laid out in the "Druckenmiller Warning," an effective bond sleeve would look something like this.

Here is what would change my mind, stated plainly so you can hold me to it. If core services excluding shelter reaccelerate, if the Employment Cost Index turns up, if real hourly earnings cross back above zero, and the quits rate rises, then the wage loop is closing, and this inflation became the durable kind while I was arguing it wasn't. Watch those four. I'd rather be corrected by data than by a client's statement.

The thing to fear was never that prices would keep climbing. It's that they'll stop climbing because nobody can afford them anymore, and labor's share of output has been telling us for twenty-five years exactly which of those two we're heading toward.

title: Another Tanker Ablaze As Iran Digs In And Trump Talks Non-Nuclear Mother Of All Bombs Threat
desc:
Another Tanker Ablaze As Iran Digs In And Trump Talks Non-Nuclear Mother Of All Bombs Threat

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Friday once again affirmed his country is not ready to give in to force, no matter how much military pressure or sanctions it faces from Washington.

He issued the words from Yerevan, Armenia, on the sidelines of the Leaders' Summit on Biodiversity. Pezeshkian said US-led sanctions "are beyond humanitarian frameworks and [US] attacks in recent months are unjustifiable and inhumane."

"Iran is not seeking nuclear weapons, and we consider the destructive propaganda against our country to be lies," he added, as quoted by Iran’s semiofficial Tasnim News Agency.

Pezeshkian then stressed: "We have always been ready to talk. They think they can make us surrender, but we will not give in to force."

During an interview with Newsmax on Thursday, President Trump reiterated some of his key rationales for going to war, and Iran's leader seemed to be directly responding to some of what Trump had to say.

"We want to make it so that they will never have a nuclear weapon, because if they had it, they would use it, in my opinion, instantaneously," Trump had said, but also again claimed the conflict would be over soon. There was also this interesting exchange with the Newsmax journalist in reference to the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb or MOAB, 'Mother of All Bombs' in Iran:

"Well, the mother of all bombs is not nuclear," Trump said.

Host Rob Finnerty asked, "Not tactical nuclear?"

"No, it's not nuclear at all. This is just an extremely large bomb," Trump said. "It's like a tiny nuclear bomb. The mother of all bombs is one big bomb, but it's not nuclear."

Trump did not say whether he had authorized the weapon's use, nor did he identify a potential target.

"The Iran war will be over very soon. It's going to end very soon," he said, while asserting that Iran is currently negotiating with the US. This seems merely a reference to messages being passed through mediators.

According to @CNN, Trump is considering using MOABs against Pickaxe nuclear site. I would not be dismissive of the idea as CSIS expert was on Thursday’s Erin Burnett. The rationale of using a MOAB is that the blast is so violent that it can overcome typical blast traps of tunnel entrances. It is like a small nuke; it is difficult to engineer entrances to withstand that level of a blast. The goal may be the confirmed closure of known access routes at Pickaxe, creating a monitored condition. Reopening is an observable change requiring action. That can be valuable even when the condition of the underground chambers would remain unknown. Moreover, MOABs would destroy surface support structures and utilities. Monitored closure, with lack of information about activities inside, has been the situation for months at Esfahan Mtn complex and the underground Natanz enrichment plant. So MOABs could put Pickaxe in the same condition as the other two nuclear sites. Note: Fordow was destroyed by earth penetrators, GBU-57s, reaching the underground halls via crashing through ventilation systems. While we have discovered probable ventilation shafts at Pickaxe, it is uncertain how they reach the main underground halls. But a MOAB on a ventilation shaft may be worth trying, if there is one to spare. The huge blast would be on the surface. Pickaxe is an isolated site, so neighboring communities would be unlikely to be affected by the blast.

— David Albright (@DAVIDHALBRIGHT1) October 16, 2026

That's when Trump threw out the following dubious line: "They've asked us to please stop. And we do, because we're negotiating with them." He also noted that he does not foresee sending US ground troops into Iran, despite some Congressional leaders expressing concern over an extended quagmire.

But as for ramped-up Iranian attacks on international shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, this certainly hasn't stopped, but instead has reached record levels this month.

In the latest Friday incident, Iran's navy has announced an oil tanker "caught fire" after trying to cross a "restricted area" in the Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian navy surveillance teams "discovered and identified a violating oil tanker that had caught fire in the restricted area," state TV said. It described the tanker "turned off its tracking systems and attempted to cross the prohibited area in the Sea of Oman."

The navy "emphasizes that the consequences of uncoordinated movements in prohibited routes and areas are creating insecurity and many dangers for other vessels," the statement said.

Another tanker is burning in the Gulf of Oman. Iranian Navy: the vessel had shut off its tracking systems and was moving through a prohibited area east of the Strait of Hormuz when monitoring teams spotted it. Tasnim. https://t.co/meouGpzngL

— Open Source Intel (@Osint613) October 16, 2026

Ultimately, the situation still looks stuck and stalemated, but the big question will remain whether Trump has the stomach to take some kind of military action before and not after the November midterm elections (which he has threatened).

Iranian attacks on shipping have now surpassed two dozen instances just half-way through the month of October alone, but there's yet to be a direct US military response, other than occasional attacks on 'illicit' Iran-linked shipping in the same waters.

title: Federal Judge Tosses Ex-CIA Chief Brennan's 'Speculative' Lawsuit Against Trump Admin
desc:
Federal Judge Tosses Ex-CIA Chief Brennan's 'Speculative' Lawsuit Against Trump Admin

Authored by Debra Heine via American Greatness,

A federal judge on Thursday threw out former CIA Director John Brennan's lawsuit, which sought to compel the Trump administration to preserve records for his defense against potential criminal charges, ruling that he lacked standing.

The Department of Justice is investigating claims that Brennan and other national security officials conspired to undermine President Donald Trump.

The suit, filed in July 2026, sought to compel the Justice Department to retain investigative records so Brennan could prove any indictment against him was the result of vindictive or selective prosecution by the Trump administration.

Judge Jia Cobb, a Clinton-appointed judge, described Brennan's allegations of political targeting as "deeply concerning," but determined the claimed injury was "speculative" and not yet imminent, as no indictment has been filed.

Brennan was President Barack Obama's CIA director from March 2013 to January 2017, and before that, Obama's counterterrorism adviser.

He is facing indictment in at least two investigations: the broader "grand conspiracy" probe into the 2016 election interference inquiry and a separate case regarding alleged false statements made to Congress in 2023.

Prosecutors in the Southern District of Florida are examining allegations that Obama and Biden-era intelligence and law enforcement officials conspired to deprive President Trump of his civil rights through various investigations, from the 2016 Russia probe and the intelligence community assessment to the Mar-a-Lago classified documents case and related matters.

According to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee, Brennan "made numerous willfully and intentionally false statements of material fact" during his testimony in 2023, including:

  • Falsely denying that the CIA relied on the discredited Steele dossier in drafting the post-2016 election Intelligence Community Assessment; and

  • Falsely testifying when he told the Committee that the CIA opposed including the Steele dossier in the Intelligence Community Assessment (ICA).

  • These statements were contradicted by the record established by the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence (HPSCI) and the CIA, the committee stated in a press release in October 2025.

Newly declassified documents show:

  • A CIA officer drafted the annex containing a summary of the dossier;

  • Brennan made the ultimate decision, along with then-FBI Director James Comey, to include information from the dossier in the ICA; and

  • Brennan overruled senior CIA officers who objected to the inclusion of the dossier material.

The former CIA director argued in his lawsuit that because he planned to contest any prosecution that arises from the DOJ's probes as vindictive and selective, internal records and communications would be needed to establish that in court.

Brennan alleged that President Trump had singled him out in retaliation for his role in the Russian collusion hoax.

Cobb appeared to that aspect of Brennan's case seriously, saying that "if he was eventually able to prove those allegations true, that would certainly suggest that his potential prosecution is vindictive."

But at this point, the judge said it remains to be seen that Brennan is facing enough harm to bring the lawsuit.

"Even taking all of Brennan's allegations to be truthful at this stage," the judge wrote, "the injury he alleges is simply too attenuated from the actions he seeks to enjoin to warrant a finding of standing here."

title: Futures Rise As Warsh Stays Mum, Tesla "Flying Car" Interrupts AI Liquidation
desc:
Futures Rise As Warsh Stays Mum, Tesla "Flying Car" Interrupts AI Liquidation

US futures are higher, and small caps are leading, as the crowded-trade unwind that hammered chips, momentum and AI baskets all week takes a breather: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said nothing about rates at the IMF gathering in Bangkok overnight (traders took the silence as a dovish gift, cutting October hike odds to 14% from 26%), Tesla jumped 5% after Musk unveiled his "flying" Roadster, and oil slipped after Trump said Iran had asked for a halt to US attacks but then it rebounded when the market realized Trump is just lying; as a result haven demand faded and the global bond rally stalled, with 10Y yields rising 6bps to 5.12%. As of 8:00am ET, S&P futures are 0.1% higher at 7,800, Nasdaq futures are down -0.2% and Dow futures are -0.2%; Russell 2000 contracts are up 0.5%. Yesterday the S&P rose 0.3% and closed within 1% of its record high after Jensen Huang rode to CoreWeave's rescue, even as the SOX fell for a 7th straight day and the Nasdaq barely eked out a gain. Premarket, all Mag 7 names except Amazon are higher led by Tesla, while CoreWeave (-3.9%), Strategy (-2.9%) and Netflix (-2.5%) lag and the AI baskets (semis and memory) remain in the red per JPM. The day's driver is Warsh (or rather what he didn't say): with the blackout starting Saturday, the Fed chair declined to push back on rate expectations and instead talked up a "massive investment surge" from AI. In rates, Treasuries slide with a mild bear steepening (2s flat, 10s +4bps, 30s +3bps per JPM) as the rebound in global stocks clips the haven bid; bunds and gilts are also lower by about 15 ticks with UK banks in focus after reports Chancellor Healey will raise their taxes. In FX, the Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index drops 0.4%, down a second day, with the kiwi and Aussie leading G10 and the euro set to end a five-week losing run. In commodities, WTI is down 1% near $97 and Brent trades around $105 but is still headed for a second weekly gain; gold is up 0.3% at $4,184, silver gains 0.8% and copper rises 1% in London. Crypto is mixed: Bitcoin is little changed around $82,000 while Ether bounces. US economic data slate includes September import/export prices (8:30am), industrial production and capacity utilization (9:15am), the federal budget balance (2pm) and August TIC flows (4pm); Fed speaker slate includes Goolsbee on Bloomberg TV at 6pm, the last word before the blackout. There are no coupon auctions, but Treasury's primary dealer questionnaire (noon ET) ahead of the Nov. 4 refunding is worth watching.

In premarket trading, Magnificent Seven stocks are mostly higher: Tesla rises 3.6% after the EV maker unveiled its long-delayed Roadster sports car (Meta Platforms (META) +0.5%, Microsoft (MSFT) +0.5%, Alphabet (GOOGL) +0.3%, Amazon (AMZN) +0.3%, Apple (AAPL) +0.3%, Nvidia (NVDA) -0.1%)

  • Fox Corp. (FOXA) gains 3.9% after BofA upgraded the media company by two notches, to buy from underperform, citing Fox’s deal to buy Roku.
  • Mobileye Global (MBLY) climbs 4% as Citi starts coverage on the maker of software and hardware technology for automobiles with a buy rating, expecting the company to benefit from growth in autonomous driving technology.
  • Semtech Corp. (SMTC) rises 4.4% after Northland Securities upgraded the company to outperform from market perform, a move that comes in the wake of its analyst day event, where it raised its third-quarter forecast.
  • Omeros (OMER) is down 4.1% after the drug developer said an advisory committee of the European Medicines Agency issued a negative opinion on the company’s application for its narsoplimab therapy.
  • Travelers (TRV) drops 4.6% after the insurance company reported net premiums written for the third quarter that met the average analyst estimate. Revenue declined modestly year on year, while catastrophe losses rose.
  • Truist Financial (TFC) falls 2.1% after the financial services company reported third quarter taxable equivalent net interest income that came in just short of expectations.
  • Wise (WSE) falls 2.3% after the payments firm reported cross-border volumes that missed analyst expectations.
    Zeta Global (ZETA) is up 4.6% after Goldman Sachs upgraded the software company to buy from neutral, seeing potential for it to gain market share.

In other corporate news, Tesla unveiled its long-delayed new Roadster sports car (yes, the one that "flies": Newsquawk reports it uses thrusters to land after a ramp jump, does 0-60mph in under a second and enters production in 2028), sending shares of its Chinese suppliers Ningbo Xusheng, Wencan Group and Ningbo Joyson Electronic up 10% each. Thoma Bravo-backed Proofpoint agreed to buy cybersecurity company Varonis Systems for about $6.3 billion, prompting six brokers to cut Varonis to hold-equivalent. Some Anthropic investors discussed a more tempered $1.5 trillion valuation on the back of slowing revenue growth, according to Reuters, confirming our article from yesterday. Netflix is replacing its chief creative officer with veteran TV and film executive Peter Rice, Meta made one of its new AI models available for developers to download and modify, Mercedes-Benz and Nvidia extended their automated driving partnership, and City Therapeutics raised $200 million in a US IPO priced at the mid-point of its range. Meanwhile, three CoreWeave co-founders have sold $3.3 billion in shares since last year's IPO, which may explain why they look so relaxed.

After a brutal few sessions for crowded pockets of the market, including chips, momentum stocks and popular thematic baskets, futures point to a mild recovery in the final trading day of the week, Bloomberg's Before the Bell notes. Europe is on track for its biggest weekly outperformance over the S&P 500 since March as investors rotate out of the AI trade, and Asian stocks rebounded as dip buyers returned to chipmakers after a four-day selloff. The relief comes after quants suffered their worst day since August and hedge funds dumped AI stocks at the second fastest pace in a year.

The overnight catalyst was Warsh, and the most important thing was what he didn't say. With the Fed about to enter its blackout ahead of the Oct 27-28 FOMC, the Chair declined to push back on market pricing despite this week's hot CPI and PPI, saying only that since September "the world has broadly conformed to our expectations." Goldman's economists read this as a signal that the FOMC is set to pause in October, while still expecting a second and final hike in December. That is the punchline even though Bloomberg Economics' Fed Sentiment Index, which tracks the tone of Fed communications, continues to rise and is now at its most hawkish level since 2023 after Daly and Hammack warned about overlapping, long-lived supply shocks.

Then there is CoreWeave, which has become ground zero in a tug of war between investors who see rising bond yields as a potential rally killer for the AI trade and those who think compute demand will outweigh such concerns. As DB's Jim Reid recaps, CoreWeave's 5Y CDS initially widened another 76bps to 1194bps, its widest level yet, before ending 30bps tighter at 1086bps once Jensen Huang declared that "CoreWeave's strength is improving every day" (we discussed the credit fallout here and here). The stock is down another 3.9% premarket.

“Today’s rebound is partly a relief rally,” said Billy Leung, an investment strategist at Global X Management. “I’d be cautious about extrapolating today into a straight-line recovery. The fundamental AI/semiconductor story in Asia remains strong, but oil and US yields remain important constraints, so the market probably stays volatile and increasingly earnings-driven.”

The flow data shows a variety of trends: cumulative flows into tech funds are tracking a record year, according to BofA citing EPFR data, and leveraged ETF AUM is off its highs but still elevated, while the long-dated Treasury ETF has seen consecutive $1 billion outflows for the first time ever. And for those worried about narrow leadership, Bloomberg's historical analysis suggests thinner, leader-driven advances have often been followed by gains, particularly over the subsequent six to 12 months.

JPM's Market Intel desk under Andrew Tyler stays Tactically Bullish and sees "stabilization in price action" with RTY leading. The team argues that this week's price action looks more like rotation than broad-based deterioration, flagging the resilience of the equal-weight S&P, and expects the rotation to slow rather than end abruptly; it remains focused on selective dip-buying, likes Financials after generally positive large-cap bank earnings, and says all eyes are on next week's META earnings and Nvidia's GTC event. JPM's ETF desk (Jonathan Rogerson) notes the retail dip-buying impulse is "in full force": SOXL has taken in $3.2 billion over two sessions (16% of AUM created), while heavy supply in Ethereum ETFs carries "a strong scent of profit-taking."

Over at Goldman, Delta One head Rich Privorotsky calls the Asian bounce "a little lackluster relative to the scale of the selloff" and warns that "the problem remains oil, which is stubbornly high." He adds that "rates are finally beginning to reflect the same AI capex growth shock that equities have spent the week repricing." Sean Vogel's flows and positioning note puts it more bluntly: "In hindsight, the pain trade was long AI/ short bonds. Now we're watching both sides unwind." The data back that up: GS Prime's AI long/short ratio has fallen to 3.27 from a 4.34 peak (7th percentile over the past year), and NDX forward P/E is down to about 21x, the lowest since the AI cycle began in 2023. Sam Dunn on the US desk sums it up: "The AI trade is still long but now a 6 out 10 in terms of length and much cleaner than it was in Jun/July."

Elsewhere, China proposed adding advanced AI technologies to its export-control list, potentially restricting overseas transfers of AI models and chips, while Taiwan will curb AI chip exports to China as part of its US trade deal, and Beijing moved to prop up its own stock market by urging companies and state funds to buy shares while guiding some investors to curb selling. In the Gulf, CENTCOM confirmed that a container ship that sank in the Strait of Hormuz this week was struck by an Iranian projectile, Iran's navy said a "violating" tanker caught fire in a restricted zone east of Hormuz, and Trump declined to rule out using the "Mother of all Bombs" on Iran after the midterms, even as he said Tehran had asked for a halt to US attacks.

In Europe, the Stoxx 600 rises 0.6% to 643.72 with 471 members up and 122 down, heading for a third day of gains; media and autos are the best performing sectors while health care is the only one in the red. The DAX leads with a 0.9% gain and cyclicals do the heavy lifting, while the FTSE 100 lags as UK banks slide after Bloomberg reported Chancellor Healey will raise taxes on banks (the Guardian says via a 3% increase to the bank surcharge): Lloyds is down 2.3% (also cut at RBC) and NatWest 2.1%, while HSBC and Barclays are little moved. JPM's desk says Defense, Renewables, Software and Momentum Short are among the best performing baskets. Here are the biggest European movers:

  • Nestle shares rise as much as 1.5% after JPMorgan upgrades the stock to overweight, saying FY27 could be a “vintage year” for the consumer goods company.
  • Aixtron shares rise as much as 10% after the chip-equipment maker reported preliminary orders well above analyst expectations.
  • Nordex shares rise as much as 15% after the wind turbine manufacturer posted third-quarter earnings that smashed expectations and raised its margin goal for the full year.
  • Verbio shares rise as much as 11% as Jefferies upgrades the German biofuels manufacturer to buy from hold, saying the company is increasingly attractive now that its investment phase is largely behind it.
  • Brunello Cucinelli shares rose as much as 6.2% after the Italian luxury firm reported third-quarter earnings that beat expectations and raised its growth guidance for the year.
  • Man Group shares gain as much as 3.3% after the UK investment firm reported stronger-than-expected inflows for the third quarter, with growth across both alternative and long-only strategies.
  • Avanza shares declined 5.3% after the lender reported operating income for the third quarter that missed the average analyst estimate.
  • Wise shares drop as much as 2.7% after the payments firm reported cross-border volumes that missed analyst expectations.
  • Lloyds Banking Group shares fall as much as 2.7% after RBC Capital Markets downgraded the UK lender to sector-perform from outperform, noting that competition in the regional deposit market threatens to erode the benefits of its structural hedge.

Asian stocks rebounded, led by chipmakers after a four-day selloff on concerns over the AI boom, with the MSCI Asia Pacific Index jumping as much as 1.8% (Samsung, SK Hynix, BHP and Alibaba the biggest contributors), though the gauge was still on track for its worst weekly loss in more than three months. Japan's Topix and Nikkei both rose 1.9%, the Hang Seng gained 1.2% and the CSI 300 0.8% as state-backed buying returned with a record 18.8 billion yuan inflow into the E Fund CSI 300 ETF on Thursday, Taiwan's Taiex added 0.7% and the ASX 200 1.1%. Korea's Kospi, which tumbled nearly 8% on Thursday, climbed as much as ~4% and closed 2% higher at 5,668. TSMC slipped despite better-than-expected results and a strong outlook, a sign that tech sentiment remains fragile. The outlier was Indonesia, where the JCI plunged 11%, the most since January 1998, after MSCI proposed reclassifying the country from emerging-market to standalone-market status; Goldman's GIR estimates outflows of $5.0 billion to $7.8 billion depending on the scenario, and IndoGBs sold off 30bps. Goldman's Asia desk (Enna Hattori) dubbed it a "soft bounce", with flows finishing only 1.2x better to sell, and cautioned that the market "will require some fundamental reassurance before being able to regain MTD losses."

In FX, the Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index is down 0.4%, falling a second day, as traders pare bets on an October Fed hike after Warsh steered clear of any policy signals. Risk-sensitive currencies lead G10, with NZD/USD up 0.9% and AUD/USD up 0.6%; the euro rises 0.2% to around 1.1245 and is set to end a five-week losing run (ING's Francesco Pesole sees it largely confined to a 1.10-1.15 range in the coming months), and the pound hit a three-week high of 1.3337 despite the bank tax story. The yen is flat around 157.9 per dollar. In EM, Bank Indonesia intervened to support the rupiah as the MSCI shock fuels bets on a rate hike, a few days after Asian central banks dumped dollars to defend their tech currencies.

In rates, Treasuries slide, led by the long end, as the rebound in global stocks reduces the appeal of haven assets and Warsh's comments did little to alter the rate outlook; 10-year yields are up 5bps at 5.11%, with 2s little changed and the curve bear steepening, unwinding part of Thursday's 12.7bp bull flattening rally which came in spite of a PPI print that was the hottest since March 2022 (because when AI capex gets wobbly, inflation apparently stops mattering). Money markets now price a 14% chance of an October hike, down from 26% earlier. European bonds are also weaker, with bunds and gilts down about 15 ticks; gilt traders are looking for clues on how Chancellor Healey will balance spending and revenue ahead of the Oct. 28 Budget, with a bank tax the latest idea. There are no coupon auctions today, but at noon ET Treasury releases its primary dealer questionnaire ahead of the Nov. 4 refunding, and some on the Street expect 20Y and 30Y auction sizes to be cut by $3 billion each (with speculation the 20Y could be cut altogether).

The short-lived nature of the Treasury rally suggests that the safe-haven status of US bonds is continuing to wane, said Steven Barrow, head of G10 strategy at Standard Bank.

In commodities, crude is on the back foot, with WTI Dec'26 down 1.2% near the bottom of a $95.29-96.39 range and Brent Dec'26 down 0.8% within $104.91-105.94, after Trump said Iran had asked for a halt to US attacks and that negotiations are ongoing; the IEA also said member countries agreed to complete the release of 100 million barrels still outstanding from the March intervention. Even so, oil is set for a second weekly advance as mounting Middle East supply risks outweigh the reserve release: Iran's navy said a "violating" tanker caught fire east of Hormuz, Saudi Arabia and the Houthis continue to trade strikes, and Ukraine has resumed attacks on Russian refineries. It's been yet another fascinating 24 hours with CoreWeave 5yr CDS initially widening another 76bps intraday to 1194bps, its widest level yet, before turning around and ending -30bps tighter at 1086bps. This turn around was seemingly sparked by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang coming to the AI computing company’s defense amid its sharp selloff in recent days. The comments likely contributed to a broad dip buying in Tech seen during the US trading session. The Philly Semi index was down over -4% in early trading before rebounding to closing down “just” -0.88% lower but still for its 7th consecutive loss. 10yr US Treasury yields were down -12.7bps due to the risk-off and yet 378 names in the S&P 500 were higher on the day and the index managed to end up with a +0.33% gain and stay within a percent of its record high. Even the NASDAQ itself pared back its losses, having hit an intraday low of -1.44% at the open, to scrape a slight +0.08% gain. The KOSPI is back up over 4% this morning as well.

Drilling deeper into the continued AI volatility, CoreWeave's equity also recovered from being down -9.54% at the lows to close up +5.94% yesterday. In terms of other comments from Nvidia CEO Huang, which turned around the session, he noted that “CoreWeave’s strength is improving every day”, before adding “I’m optimistic. Their cost of capital is actually decreasing.” While that is true given when the company issued its current debt, the market is pointing to a higher cost of capital now and increased refinancing costs in the future, so it's one to continue to watch. I explored some of these moves in more depth in my chart of the day yesterday (link here), which showed that for now at least, AI-linked financing costs aren’t excessive relative to the rest of the credit stack but there are outliers starting to emerge. Indeed, Oracle is the other main outlier and the stock was down -8.83% at the lows yesterday before recovering to close +2.02% higher.

Overnight, Kevin Warsh has just spoken at the IMF conference and perhaps the most important thing was what he didn’t say. With the Fed about to enter its blackout ahead of the October 27-28 meeting, Warsh declined to push back against rate expectations, saying he doesn’t “prejudge meetings”, despite this week’s hotter inflation numbers. Instead, he was strikingly upbeat about the US economy, talking about a “massive investment surge” and the potentially huge productivity benefits from AI. Markets took the lack of hawkishness as good news, with October hike pricing dropping to around 15% from roughly 30% as he spoke, while S&P and Nasdaq futures are both +0.15% higher having been negative for most of the session before he spoke. Stoxx futures are +0.68% higher.

A recovery in Asian equity markets had already been in full force before Warsh but has continued after. South Korea's chip-heavy KOSPI (+4.28%) is leading gains after tumbling nearly 8% yesterday, a move that pushed the index to its lowest close since April. Elsewhere, the Nikkei (+1.83%) is also trading firmly higher, recovering a portion of Thursday's steep losses as semiconductor stocks have regained ground. Chinese equities are likewise advancing, with the Hang Seng (+1.25%), CSI 300 (+0.75%) and the Shanghai Composite (+0.95%) all higher. In contrast, Indonesia's Jakarta Composite is plunging nearly -11.0% in its steepest one-day decline since January 1998 after MSCI proposed reclassifying the country from emerging-market to standalone-market status.

Warsh's comments overnight actually followed another hawkish round of Fed speakers ahead of the upcoming Fed blackout period. Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco President Daly said that she had changed her view from earlier this year that the Fed should “look through” supply shocks, saying “Do the conventional pieces of wisdom — where our tool doesn’t really work for supply shocks and they dissipate on their own — does that really apply when the shocks are overlapping and they’re long-lived?” Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Hammack joined her in these concerns, adding that “at some point businesses start building in an expectation that more of these are going to come, and that prices are just going to keep going up.”

However the theme of the day was a big global rate rally, as the prospect of slower AI growth pushed yields lower across the board. So, the 2yr yield (-5.9bps) fell to 4.74%, whilst the 10yr yield (-12.7bps) was down to 5.06%. And this was a global pattern as well, with yields on 10yr bunds (-5.3bps), OATs (-8.5bps) and BTPs (-6.7bps) all falling over the session.

But even as bonds were rallying, a striking feature was it took place despite another batch of hawkish US data. So in other words, AI growth concerns continued to outweigh the inflation impulse when it came to yields. Most notably, there was a huge upside surprise in PPI inflation, with headline inflation up +1.3% in September (vs. +0.6% expected). In fact, it was the strongest monthly jump in producer prices since March 2022, shortly after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Moreover, the core measures were also stronger than expected, with the measure excluding food, energy and trade services up +0.5% on the month (vs. +0.3% expected). So as with the CPI, the release helped to fuel concerns that inflation was broadening out beyond energy. Taking into account the PPI and CPI components, our US econ team is projecting a +0.37% monthly increase for PCE.

The hawkish data impulse was also clear in the labour market, as the weekly initial jobless claims also remained low in the week ending October 10, coming in at just 199k (vs. 200k expected). So that kept the 4-week moving average broadly steady at 198.5k, only up slightly from its 198.25k level the previous week. In addition, the retail sales number was also stronger than expected, rising +0.8% in September (vs. +0.3% expected). So with the latest data, that left the Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow estimate at an annualised pace of +3.6% for Q3.

Earlier in Europe, markets put in a relatively stronger performance, as they remained more insulated from the AI-related issues. So the STOXX 600 (+0.38%) actually put in a second consecutive gain, taking the index to a 3-week high. That included particularly strong gains for the FTSE 100 (+1.08%) and France’s CAC 40 (+0.78%), although Italy’s FTSE MIB (-0.72%) was a relative underperformer. In the meantime, gilts saw a relative underperformance, with the 10yr yield only down -5.0bps on the day which came as the UK GDP release for August was stronger than expected. That showed GDP up +0.1% (vs. -0.1% expected), which meant the rolling 3-month growth rate was at +0.7% compared to the previous three months (vs. +0.5% expected).

Looking at the day ahead, and it’s a quiet one ahead. However, we will get data on US industrial production and capacity utilization for September. In the Euro Area, there’s also the final CPI print for September.

title: CoreWeave Founders Cashed Out $3.3 Billion Before The Meltdown
desc:
CoreWeave Founders Cashed Out $3.3 Billion Before The Meltdown

Before CoreWeave imploded, its three co-founders had been busy dumping stock, a lot of it, totaling $3.3 billion since the company's March 2025 IPO. The AI cloud provider rents access to Nvidia-powered data centers that fuel the AI circular financing scheme. Its unsecured bonds due in 2032 have crossed into distressed territory, and its five-year CDS spreads have blown out as debt levels at hyperscalers and neocloud providers come into question.

Michael Intrator, Brian Venturo and Brannin McBee sold $2.4 billion this year alone, according to Bloomberg's new report on corporate filings.

Intrator has sold more than $907 million in shares this year. McBee's sales since the IPO total $1.06 billion, equivalent to 40.4% of his undiluted stake at the listing. Venturo has sold more than $1.2 billion, representing over 35% of his original holding.

As musician Kenny Rogers once sang, "You got to know when to hold 'em, know when to fold 'em, know when to walk away, and know when to run..."

CoreWeave shares have plunged more than 50% from their May peak, erasing $15 billion of the founders' paper wealth.

title: Americans' Trust In Fellow Voters Falls To Fifty Year Low; Survey Finds
desc:
Americans' Trust In Fellow Voters Falls To Fifty Year Low; Survey Finds

Authored by Bryan Hyde via American Greatness,

Americans' trust in their fellow citizens' voting judgment has fallen to its lowest recorded level in more than five decades, according to a recently published Gallup survey.

American voters' growing distrust of political leaders and institutions now extends to one another, with Democrats and Republicans showing similar levels of skepticism.

According to Gallup, 51% of U.S. adults have a great deal or fair amount of trust in Americans as a whole to make democratic judgments - the lowest reading since Gallup began tracking the measure in 1974.

Five measures of trust in the federal government are at low points in Gallup's trends. pic.twitter.com/uwmZXcCJT0

— Gallup (@Gallup) October 14, 2026

Axios reports the distrust cuts across party lines with just 53 percent of Democrats, 51 percent of Republicans and 49 percent of independents trusting Americans' ability to make democratic decisions.

While the public's skepticism was historically aimed at political leaders and government institutions, the growing partisan divide has now caused citizens to lose faith in one another, reflecting a deeper systemic shift.

According to the Pew Research Center, public trust in the electorate's democratic judgment has been on a downward trajectory for several decades, accelerating sharply in recent years.

Trust stood at 86 percent in 1976 and 78 percent in both 2002 and 2005, but has stayed below 60percent since 2018, according to Gallup.

The Gallup survey found that Americans have more trust in their local government (67 percent) and state government (55 percent) than in their fellow citizens' democratic judgment (51 percent), according to Axios.

Democrats are more likely than Republicans and independents to trust both local and state governments.

Gallup reports Republicans still largely retain trust in the federal government, albeit somewhat less than a year ago.

The survey also revealed that 42 percent of Americans say they trust politicians who hold or seek public office, while 33 percent trust the news media.

The erosion of peer-to-peer trust is particularly concerning to political scientists who say the trend poses a unique challenge to democratic norms.

When voters view the opposing side not merely as political rivals but as fundamentally incapable of sound democratic decision-making, it undermines the willingness of the defeated party to accept election outcomes as valid.

Gallup surveyed 1,000 U.S. adults by landline and cellphone Sept. 1-17, 2026 with a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points.

title: Beijing Tightens Grip On Solar Exports: Will Trump Play America's Quartz Card?
desc:
Beijing Tightens Grip On Solar Exports: Will Trump Play America's Quartz Card?

Beijing's new restrictions on advanced solar technologies and equipment suggest the Trump-Xi meeting in Washington did little to ease trade tensions. The new measures aim to preserve China's technological advantage as the US and India expand domestic solar manufacturing. This reinforces ongoing concerns about critical materials, where Beijing has placed export controls on tungsten, germanium, gallium, and antimony.

Bloomberg cites a statement released by China's Ministry of Commerce earlier this morning announcing that it would add 12 solar-related technologies and core equipment to its export-control list, citing national security concerns. The changes form part of a broader revision covering 40 technologies, including AI and biopharmaceuticals.

"In recent years, the application of solar technology in sensitive fields such as aerospace, national defense, unmanned equipment, and high-security-level infrastructure has been continuously expanding," the ministry said in the statement.

The statement continued, "The national security risks that may be caused by the export of solar technology have been constantly rising. It is necessary to implement timely and appropriate supervision."

The measures include a ban on exports of production technology for perovskite and solar modules, advanced technologies that offer higher efficiency and potential use in space-based solar power. Restrictions will also apply to certain technologies used to produce polysilicon, a key solar-panel material.

According to BloombergNEF analysts, the new controls could complicate efforts to diversify the global solar supply chain. Manufacturers in the US and India still depend on China for some critical materials, equipment, and technologies.

The question now is how the Trump administration will respond, if it can.

Trump administration trade officials could restrict exports of US high-purity quartz to China through export controls and licensing requirements.

China's solar dominance remains vulnerable to restrictions on US-sourced high-purity quartz, giving Trump potential leverage.

title: For restaurants Covid-19 was a crisis – pandemic loans are proving a disaster
desc:
Low-interest loans kept many eateries afloat. But the industry never recovered enough for them to repay the debt

For almost 20 years, Jai Mazumdar has served vegetarian curries, samosas, gulab jamun and other Indian delicacies at Spice N Curry, a cafe and grocery nestled inside a modest strip mall near Florida International University (FIU) in Miami. When the Covid-19 pandemic devastated his business, as it did with so many restaurants, Mazumdar took out a $370,000 economic injury disaster loan (EIDL) from the federal government in early 2021.

At the time, it provided a desperately needed lifeline. He was confident that once business returned to normal he could begin repaying the 30-year loan, which came with a low 3.75% interest rate and a 30-month deferment period. But when his business didn’t recover, the disaster loan turned out to be a disaster of its own.

title: Will Trump’s economy sink Republicans in the US midterm elections? Our reporters answered your questions
desc:
The high cost of living has Americans angrier than ever. Guardian reporters answered your questions about the US economy ahead of November

  • Sign up for the Stakes newsletter for more midterms coverage

  • Send us your questions on Trump’s immigration agenda ahead of the midterms

LucccA asks: Why are labor unions in the US still not as well-organized compared to the rest of the world? I know there was a push against them in the past—does that still have an effect today? Also, why are there so many right-leaning unions in the US?

Michael: A lot of reasons. The US has low union density compared to other wealthy nations, currently at 10.0%, and that has been on a precipitous decline for the past few decades for a variety of reasons that include anti-union and union busting campaigns, outdated labor laws where employers often retaliate for union organizing or delay bargaining for years, as we are seeing with Starbucks, where there is no union contract after nearly five years since the first store won its union election in December 2021.Right to work laws in the US also undermine labor unions and starve them of resources. To the extent that there are right leaning labor unions in the US, they typically are law enforcement unions that consistently endorse and back Republican candidates despite the Republican Party in the US opposing collective bargaining. Some unions like the Teamsters have been making efforts to get Republicans to support legislation and in turn receive endorsements from the union, and this has shown up this election cycle with the Teamsters endorsing Republicans like Congressman Max Miller or Kansas Senator Roger Marshall, who are both facing very competitive re-election battles.

Heather: There’s a bunch of ideas floating around on cutting costs for groceries, healthcare and energy bills. A key thing Democrats are promising if they regain power in Congress is to wrestle back authority on trade and repeal Trump’s tariffs, which would lower what it costs compaines to import. A second is to advance a vote to stop the war in Iran, which could calm fuel prices. If Democrats retake the Senate, expect Elizabeth Warren to become chair of the powerful banking committe, and push forward some curbs on private equity investments. And Democrats have been coalescing around more government funding for childcare, a notable move to the left in recent years. Hakeem Jeffries, who will be House Speaker if Democrats win there, is promising to reinstate ACA tax cuts and roll back Medicaid cuts, but the party is divided on Medicare For All, with DSA candidates making promises on the campaign trail and more centrist Dems being pretty quiet.

Republicans running for Congress have been talking a lot about ways to lower gas prices, especially suspending the fuel tax, and shaving utility bills by making tech companies and other big users pay more. Some have promised to curb Trump’s tariffs, including Michigan’s Mike Rogers, and others are proposing suspending data center building after public backlash.

title: The global economy is muddling through against the odds. But a storm is coming | Larry Elliott
desc:
Finance ministers gathering for the IMF annual meeting know the need for multilateral cooperation to deal with many crises. There is little chance of that

Not much has gone right for the global economy this year, and plenty has gone wrong. Two big regional wars are destabilising prices and supply chains everywhere. Businesses and consumers are feeling the effects of a serious energy shock. Rising inflation has made it a lot more expensive for governments to finance their debts. China and the US are at loggerheads over trade.

Yet, so far, the impact has been modest. It is something of a miracle that the finance ministers and central bank governors gathered for this year’s annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Bangkok are not having to deal with a full-blown crisis. This is not like the autumn of 2008, when the meetings took place during the worst of the global banking meltdown.

Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnist
